Forms

18 patterns

Data entry is where trust is won or lost fastest, a form that fights back gets abandoned.

Type: debounced save cycle
idle
01

Autosave

Firing a save on every keystroke floods the network with redundant requests, so debounce writes to one clean save after roughly a second of pause. Status needs to be an honest state machine: idle, saving, saved, error, never a lie like a permanent “Saved” label that stopped being true the moment the network dropped. Queue edits made offline and replay them oldest-first on reconnect, and guard unsaved work with beforeunload so a stray tab-close doesn’t silently lose a paragraph.

  • ✓Queue edits offline, replay oldest-first on reconnect
  • ×Silent last-write-wins across two open tabs
JS
let saveTimer, status = 'idle';

function onEdit(value) {
  setStatus('idle');
  clearTimeout(saveTimer);
  saveTimer = setTimeout(() => save(value), 1000); // debounced, not per-keystroke
}

async function save(value) {
  setStatus('saving');
  try { await api.save(value); setStatus('saved'); }
  catch { setStatus('error'); queueOffline(value); } // replayed oldest-first on reconnect
}

window.addEventListener('beforeunload', (e) => {
  if (status === 'idle') e.preventDefault(); // unsaved edit pending
});
Presets cover ~90% of real use
02

Date Pickers

Presets (Today, Last 7 days, Last 30 days, This month) cover roughly 90% of real use, so lead with them and treat a full custom range as the fallback, not the default view. Show two months side by side so a range can cross a month boundary without extra navigation, and support full keyboard control including month/year jumps for anyone picking a date far from today rather than forcing repeated “next” clicks. On mobile, hand the job to the platform's native date input rather than shipping a custom calendar; reach for a custom one on desktop only once the native control genuinely can't do what the screen needs. Either way, keep a typed text field as a real fallback, and let it parse plain language such as “tomorrow” or “next friday” rather than demanding a strict format.

  • ✓Two months side by side, ranges cross boundaries
  • ✓A typed, parsed text field for far-past dates (birthdates), not arrow-only navigation
  • ✓Native date input on mobile; a custom calendar only where native genuinely falls short
  • ×Repeated “next” clicks for a nearby date
Concrete cost of arrow-only navigation: a calendar that opens on today's date makes a 1994 birthday cost roughly 390 clicks of a single arrow. Nobody does that, they abandon the form.
JS
const PRESETS = [
  { label: 'Today', range: () => [today(), today()] },
  { label: 'Last 7 days', range: () => [daysAgo(7), today()] },
  { label: 'Last 30 days', range: () => [daysAgo(30), today()] },
  { label: 'This month', range: () => [startOfMonth(), today()] },
]; // custom range is a separate, secondary tab, not the default view

picker.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'PageUp') shiftMonth(e.shiftKey ? -12 : -1); // shift+PageUp = year jump
  if (e.key === 'PageDown') shiftMonth(e.shiftKey ? 12 : 1);
});
Simulate an upload
Drop a file, or
quarterly_report.pdf
0%
03

File Upload UX

Upload is a whole system of states, not a bare <input type="file">: drag-over feedback, honest per-file progress, error recovery, a preview once it lands, and a queue when multiple files go at once. Support drag-and-drop and a plain click-to-browse button together, never just one; not everyone drags, and not everyone notices a drop zone is a drop zone. Show percent complete plus a time-remaining estimate rather than an indeterminate spinner, since spinners give no sense of whether a large file is almost done or barely started. Once a file lands, let someone remove it before they submit, the same way they'd delete a wrong attachment from an email. On failure, retry inline with the same file still loaded in memory; forcing a full re-select after a failed 200MB upload is a real cost to whoever hit it.

  • ✓Drag-and-drop and click-to-browse both supported, not just one
  • ✓Percent + time-remaining, not a bare spinner
  • ✓Remove a file before submit, the same as deleting a wrong email attachment
  • ×Forcing a full re-select after a failure
JS
dropzone.addEventListener('dragover', e => { e.preventDefault(); dropzone.classList.add('drag'); });
dropzone.addEventListener('drop', e => {
  e.preventDefault(); dropzone.classList.remove('drag');
  [...e.dataTransfer.files].forEach(uploadWithProgress);
});

function uploadWithProgress(file) {
  const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
  const startedAt = performance.now();
  xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => {
    const pct = Math.round((e.loaded / e.total) * 100);
    const rate = e.loaded / ((performance.now() - startedAt) / 1000);
    const etaSec = Math.round((e.total - e.loaded) / rate);
    updateRow(file, { pct, etaSec });
  };
  xhr.onerror = () => updateRow(file, { error: true, retry: () => uploadWithProgress(file) }); // file stays loaded
  xhr.open('POST', '/upload'); xhr.send(toFormData(file));
}
One field, six states
04

Form Field States

Every field in a design system needs all six states actually designed, not improvised: default, focus, error, success, disabled, and loading. The label lives outside the field permanently. A placeholder pretending to be a label disappears the instant someone starts typing, so by the time they’re three fields deep they’ve forgotten what field four was asking for. Above the field is the right default placement: it scans fastest, works best on mobile, and survives translation into a longer language without crowding the control. A floating label that sits inside the field until focus is fine in genuinely tight spaces, but never on a multi-line textarea, where it collides with the first line typed. An inline label to the left of its control only earns its place on a wide settings page where label and control sit side by side on purpose. Placeholder text standing in as the only label is never acceptable at any width, it disappears exactly when someone needs it most. Errors need to combine colour with an icon and a written message; colour alone (a red border) is invisible to a colour-blind user and easy to miss at a glance regardless. Mark the exception, not the norm: label an optional field with a plain “(optional)” suffix rather than flagging every required field with an asterisk, since most fields in a well-scoped form should be required by design.

  • ✓Label outside the field, never placeholder-as-label
  • ✓Above the field by default; floating only in tight spaces, never on a textarea; inline-left only on a wide settings page
  • ✓“(optional)” on the exception, not an asterisk on every required field
  • ×Border-only red, invisible to colour-blind users
CSS
.field { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 6px; }
.field label { font-size: 13px; font-weight: 600; } /* always visible, never a placeholder */

.field input { border: 1px solid var(--border); transition: border-color 150ms; }
.field input:focus { border-color: var(--accent); outline: 2px solid var(--accent-a20); }
.field.error input { border-color: var(--error); }
.field.success input { border-color: var(--success); }
.field input:disabled { background: var(--surface-muted); cursor: not-allowed; }

.field-msg.error { color: var(--error); display: flex; gap: 4px; align-items: center; }
.field-msg.error::before { content: '⚠'; } /* icon, not colour alone */
Blur to validate, then live once errored
05

Form Validation Timing

Validate on blur, once someone has finished with a field and moved on, not on every keystroke, which flags an email as invalid while it’s still half-typed, and not held back entirely until submit, which dumps every problem on the form at once. Once a field has errored, switch to live revalidation on every keystroke for that field alone, so the error clears the instant it’s actually fixed. Confirm correct fields too with a quiet success state, not just the broken ones; it tells someone they can stop worrying about that field. The message itself has three parts in order: what’s wrong, why it matters, how to fix it. So “Invalid email” becomes “This email is missing the @ symbol” or, for a taken address, “We already have an account with this email, sign in instead?”

  • ✓Live revalidation once a field has errored
  • ✓Message states what’s wrong and how to fix it, not just “Invalid”
  • ×Dumping every error at submit, all at once
JS
const errored = new Set();

input.addEventListener('blur', () => validate(input)); // first pass: on blur only
input.addEventListener('input', () => {
  if (errored.has(input.name)) validate(input); // live only once it has errored
});

function validate(field) {
  const ok = field.checkValidity();
  field.closest('.field').classList.toggle('error', !ok);
  field.closest('.field').classList.toggle('success', ok && field.value !== '');
  ok ? errored.delete(field.name) : errored.add(field.name);
}
Type a card number
06

Input Masking

Group long numbers into readable chunks as they’re typed (a card number in 4-digit blocks, a phone number split by area code), and detect the card brand from the leading digit to show the right icon before the number is even complete. The caret needs to land after the character that was just typed, not jump to the end of the field, which is the usual bug in a hand-rolled mask. Store the raw digits internally and only format for display; validating the masked format on the very first keystroke rejects a perfectly valid number that just isn’t finished yet.

  • ✓Store raw digits, display the formatted grouping
  • ×Validating format on the very first keystroke
JS
function maskCardNumber(input) {
  const caretFromEnd = input.value.length - input.selectionStart;
  const digits = input.value.replace(/\D/g, '').slice(0, 16);
  input.value = digits.replace(/(\d{4})(?=\d)/g, '$1 '); // raw digits stored separately
  const pos = input.value.length - caretFromEnd;
  input.setSelectionRange(pos, pos); // caret follows the just-typed char
}

function detectBrand(digits) {
  if (/^4/.test(digits)) return 'visa';
  if (/^5[1-5]/.test(digits)) return 'mastercard';
  if (/^3[47]/.test(digits)) return 'amex';
  return null; // shown before the number is even complete
}
Type or paste a 6-digit code
07

OTP Input

Model the code as a single string in state, not six independent input boxes each tracking their own value; six-box implementations are where paste handling reliably breaks. Treat paste as the primary entry path rather than an edge case, since most codes are copied from an SMS or authenticator app, not typed digit by digit. Auto-advance focus to the next box as each digit lands, let backspace on an empty box jump back to the previous one, and gate resend behind a visible countdown so the retry button isn’t just sitting there inviting spam.

Tag the input with inputmode="numeric" and autocomplete="one-time-code". Together they are what let a phone autofill the SMS code.

Colour is reserved for verdicts. Keep the UI neutral (light and grey) while the code is being entered: green appears only when the code is correct and red only when it is wrong, and those two are the only status colours in play. Keep those status colours separate from the brand accent, and see Color Accessibility (Visual, entry 03) for the second-signal rule that any colour-coded verdict still needs.

  • ✓Auto-advance focus, backspace jumps back a box
  • ✓inputmode="numeric" and autocomplete="one-time-code" on the input, so phones autofill the SMS code
  • ✓Neutral UI until a verdict: green only when the code is correct, red only when it is wrong
  • ×A wrong code sitting silently, no shake/refocus
  • ×Green or red on the boxes before the code has been judged
A flourish and an opinion, not a recommended pattern. One popular animation moves the CSS transform-origin to the hub of a ring, so a plain rotate() draws an exact circle and the whole spin is two keyframes (rotate(0deg) to rotate(450deg) on an eased, wind-up-then-brake curve), with no path sampling. That is a sound, established CSS technique, worth knowing for decorative motion. As a UX choice it is a flourish: the choreography (four boxes swing onto a dotted ring, spin a turn and a quarter, settle into one green tile) adds about a second of delay after the person has already typed the code, and it is widely received as too much and machine-made. It is an animation demo, not a rule, and it is not part of this standard. How it is received is listed with the other tells in AI Slop: What Not To Do (entry 05).
JS
let code = ''; // one string, not six independent box values

boxes[0].addEventListener('paste', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  code = (e.clipboardData.getData('text').match(/\d/g) || []).slice(0, 6).join('');
  syncBoxes(); // paste is the primary path, not an edge case
  if (code.length === 6) submit(code);
});

boxes.forEach((box, i) => box.addEventListener('input', () => {
  code = code.slice(0, i) + box.value + code.slice(i + 1);
  if (box.value && boxes[i + 1]) boxes[i + 1].focus(); // auto-advance
}));
boxes.forEach((box, i) => box.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'Backspace' && !box.value && boxes[i - 1]) boxes[i - 1].focus(); // jump back
}));

// phones autofill the SMS code when the input is tagged like this:
// <input inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code">

// colour is reserved for verdicts: neutral while typing, green only if the code is correct, red only if it is wrong
// .otp-box.ok { border-color: var(--ok); }  .otp-box.bad { border-color: var(--bad); }  (the only two status colours)
Type a password
  • At least 12 characters
  • Upper and lower case
  • At least one number
08

Password Field UX

Real strength is entropy: length matters far more than a symbol checkbox, which just pushes everyone toward “Password1!”-shaped passwords. Show the actual requirements checklist live as someone types, with each line ticking green the moment it’s satisfied, rather than surfacing the whole list only after a failed submit. Always pair a visibility toggle with a one-tap generate-a-strong-password option, and never block paste; a blocked paste breaks every password manager and pushes people toward weaker, memorable passwords instead.

  • ✓Visibility toggle + a one-tap generated password
  • ×Hiding requirements until after a failed submit
JS
const RULES = [
  { test: v => v.length >= 12, label: 'At least 12 characters' }, // length > symbol tricks
  { test: v => /[A-Z]/.test(v) && /[a-z]/.test(v), label: 'Upper and lower case' },
  { test: v => /\d/.test(v), label: 'At least one number' },
];

input.addEventListener('input', () => { // live checklist, shown from the first keystroke
  RULES.forEach((rule, i) => checklistItems[i].classList.toggle('met', rule.test(input.value)));
});

toggleBtn.addEventListener('click', () => input.type = input.type === 'password' ? 'text' : 'password');
generateBtn.addEventListener('click', () => { input.value = generateStrongPassword(16); input.dispatchEvent(new Event('input')); });
// no paste-blocking handler, password managers must be able to fill this field
Drag or use arrow keys
40% discount
09

Range Sliders

Fill the track up to the thumb so the value reads at a glance without needing the number label, and make the entire row a draggable hit area rather than a thin 4px hairline that’s genuinely hard to grab on a touch screen. Snap to defined steps whenever clean values actually matter (percentages, price bands), and float the live numeric value in a small bubble above the thumb while dragging so precision doesn’t depend on reading a separate, disconnected label.

  • ✓Float the live value above the thumb while dragging
  • ×A slider that can’t be driven by arrow keys
CSS + JS
input[type=range] {
  -webkit-appearance: none; height: 32px; /* full row is the hit area, not a thin track */
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--accent) var(--fill, 0%), var(--track) var(--fill, 0%));
  border-radius: 999px;
}
input[type=range]::-webkit-slider-thumb {
  -webkit-appearance: none; width: 20px; height: 20px; border-radius: 50%;
  background: var(--accent); box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / .2);
}

slider.addEventListener('input', () => {
  const pct = ((slider.value - slider.min) / (slider.max - slider.min)) * 100;
  slider.style.setProperty('--fill', pct + '%');
  bubble.textContent = slider.value; bubble.style.left = pct + '%'; // floats above the thumb
});
// native input[type=range] already supports arrow-key stepping, don't override onkeydown
Instant toggle vs. explicit Save
Email notifications
Applies instantly
Organization name
Acme Pty Ltd
10

Settings System

Match the apply model to what’s actually at stake: a low-risk toggle (dark mode, notifications) applies instantly with no Save button, while a high-stakes identity field (email, billing) needs an explicit Save so a stray click can’t silently change something significant. Group settings by the task someone came to do, not by how the database happens to be organised, and make the whole page searchable once it passes roughly fifteen options. A destructive setting change belongs in a clearly separated danger zone, type-to-confirm gated.

  • ✓Group by task, make it searchable
  • ×One flat list ordered by the data model
JS
const SETTINGS = [
  { key: 'darkMode', group: 'Appearance', apply: 'instant' },   // low-risk, no Save button
  { key: 'email', group: 'Account', apply: 'explicit' },     // identity field, needs Save
  { key: 'deleteAccount', group: 'Danger zone', apply: 'confirm-typed' },
];

function onChange(setting, value) {
  if (setting.apply === 'instant') return save(setting.key, value); // fires immediately
  if (setting.apply === 'explicit') markDirty(setting.key, value);   // waits for Save click
  if (setting.apply === 'confirm-typed') openTypeToConfirm(setting);   // e.g. type account email to delete
}
Real Next / Back through 3 steps
Personal
Full name, email, validated before Next unlocks
Shipping
Address, city, postcode

11

Stepper Wizard

Chunk a long form by meaning (Personal, Shipping, Payment, Review), not by an arbitrary field count that splits a logically single group across two steps. Validate inside each step and block the Next button until it’s valid, so a step-one mistake never surfaces for the first time at step four after everything else has already been filled in. Persist state across Back navigation and even a page refresh; losing a half-completed multi-step form to an accidental reload is one of the more infuriating things software still does.

  • ✓Validate inside each step, block Next until valid
  • ×Surfacing a step-one error only at step four
JS
const STEPS = ['personal', 'shipping', 'payment', 'review']; // chunked by meaning
let stepIndex = 0;
const formState = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('wizard-draft') || '{}'); // survives refresh

function goNext() {
  if (!validateStep(STEPS[stepIndex], formState)) return; // blocked here, not at review
  stepIndex++;
  localStorage.setItem('wizard-draft', JSON.stringify(formState));
  render();
}
function goBack() { stepIndex--; render(); } // formState untouched, nothing lost
Click either: instant vs. async
instant
simulated async
12

Toggle Anatomy

A good toggle morphs over roughly 250ms: the rail colour, the knob position, and the knob’s shadow all move together on the same curve, rather than snapping instantly between on and off. For an async toggle backed by a real API call, flip optimistically the instant it’s tapped and show a small spinner inside the knob itself while the request is in flight, rolling back with a shake if it fails. It must remain a real, focusable, keyboard- and screen-reader-operable control, built on <button role="switch"> or a checkbox, never a plain <div> with a click handler.

  • ✓Rail colour, knob position, shadow move together
  • ×A toggle that skips keyboard/screen readers
CSS + JS
.toggle { position: relative; width: 44px; height: 26px; border-radius: 999px;
  background: var(--rail-off); transition: background 250ms ease; }
.toggle[aria-checked="true"] { background: var(--accent); }
.toggle .knob { position: absolute; top: 3px; left: 3px; width: 20px; height: 20px;
  border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / .3);
  transition: transform 250ms ease; } /* same curve as the rail */
.toggle[aria-checked="true"] .knob { transform: translateX(18px); }

toggle.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const next = toggle.getAttribute('aria-checked') !== 'true';
  toggle.setAttribute('aria-checked', String(next)); // optimistic flip
  try { await api.setSetting(next); }
  catch { toggle.setAttribute('aria-checked', String(!next)); } // roll back on failure
});
toggle.addEventListener('keydown', e => { if (e.key === ' ' || e.key === 'Enter') toggle.click(); });
Checked radio, zero JS: :has() styles the card
Right card: .plan:has(:checked), no click handler
13

:has() Parent Queries

The :has() relational pseudo-class lets a parent's style react to what's inside it, closing off a whole category of state that used to require JavaScript just to toggle a class. Five uses worth knowing: selection, a pricing-plan card highlights itself with .plan:has(:checked) when its own radio is selected, no click handler. Validation, a field wrapper turns red with .field:has(:user-invalid) the moment its input fails constraint validation, live, with zero onChange/useState. Layout, a shell can switch to a two-column grid only when a specific child exists, e.g. .app:has(aside), so layout follows what's actually in the DOM instead of a JS-tracked boolean prop. Quantity, a grid can query its own child count, e.g. .plans:has(:nth-child(n+5)), and switch to a denser layout once it crosses a threshold: a quantity query in pure CSS. Document-level reaction, body:has(dialog[open]) can lock background scroll and dim the app the instant any dialog anywhere opens, in one rule, instead of a JS class toggled on every open/close. Browser support is broad but not universal (Chrome 105+, Safari 15.4+, Firefox 121+, Edge 105+); check the project's actual support target before relying on it for anything load-bearing.

  • ✓.plan:has(:checked) instead of a click handler + class toggle
  • ✓:has(:user-invalid) for live validation styling with zero JS state
  • ✓Check real browser-support targets before depending on :has()
  • ×Reaching for a JS state toggle when the parent can just query its own children
CSS
/* 01, selection: the card reacts to its own radio, no click handler */
.plan:has(:checked) { border-color: var(--accent); }

/* 02, validation: the wrapper reacts to its own input's validity, live */
.field:has(:user-invalid) { border-color: var(--err); }

/* 03, layout: follows the DOM, not a JS-tracked prop */
.app:has(aside) { grid-template-columns: 280px 1fr; }

/* 04, quantity: the grid counts its own children */
.plans:has(:nth-child(n+5)) { --density: compact; }

/* 05, document-level: any open dialog locks + dims the whole app */
body:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; }
body:has(dialog[open]) .app { opacity: .4; pointer-events: none; }
Same 6 fields, grouped by mental model
Ungrouped, one flat list
About you
Notifications
Grouped, 2 named sections
14

Form Field Grouping

More than seven visible fields on one screen is a cognitive-load problem before it’s a layout problem. Reach for progressive disclosure, a multi-step wizard, or a collapsed “advanced” section, or go back and ask whether every field is actually needed rather than collected just in case. Group what remains by mental model, not by the shape of the database table behind it: “About you” / “How to reach you” / “Your preferences” reads as a conversation; user_id, created_at, metadata does not. Three to five fields per group is the ceiling. Past that, split into two groups with their own heading rather than one long one. Every field should carry a default that’s right for most people: country read from locale, currency matched to that country, a date field defaulting to today, time zone taken from the browser rather than asked for, notification preferences starting at “important only” rather than “all”, and any privacy choice starting on the more private option. None of that applies to a destructive or expensive choice, which is never defaulted on (“Yes, subscribe me to everything” starts unchecked, always).

  • ✓Groups named by task/mental model (“Shipping”, “Billing”), not by table name
  • ✓3-5 fields per group before splitting into a new one
  • ✓Smart defaults for the 80% case (locale, currency, today's date, browser time zone); never for a destructive or costly choice
  • ×15 fields visible at once with no grouping, wizard, or progressive disclosure
The submit button carries the same discipline. Its label names the action, “Create account” or “Send invoice”, never a bare “Submit”. It sits bottom right of the form on desktop and full width, sticky to the bottom, on mobile. A disabled state only ever appears with a visible reason attached, never a greyed-out button with no explanation. Loading swaps in a spinner and a “Saving…” label. After success, either navigate somewhere new or show a clear confirmation, never neither, silence after submitting reads as a failure even when it wasn't one.
JSX
// grouped by mental model, 3-5 fields per group, 7-field ceiling before splitting into steps
<fieldset><legend>About you</legend>
  <Field label="Full name" />
  <Field label="Work email" />
</fieldset>
<fieldset><legend>Notifications</legend>
  <Field label="Frequency" defaultValue="important only" /> {/* smart default, not "all" */}
</fieldset>
<details><summary>Add company info (optional)</summary>
  <fieldset><Field label="Company" optional /><Field label="Job title" optional /></fieldset>
</details>

15

Field Control Thresholds

The right control for a choice depends on how many options it holds, and the thresholds are concrete enough to apply without debate. Two or three options fit a segmented control or a small radio group, visible all at once with no extra tap. Four to seven options still fit visible radio buttons; that beats a dropdown at this size because every option is scannable without opening anything. Eight to fifteen options is where a dropdown earns its place, once the list is too long to show comfortably but still short enough to scroll by eye. Sixteen or more calls for a searchable combobox, and past fifty a dropdown should hand off to async search rather than trying to render the whole list at once. A checkbox and a toggle are not interchangeable either: a checkbox implies the change only takes effect once the form is explicitly saved, a toggle implies it applies the instant it's flipped, and mixing both metaphors on one screen makes someone guess which promise a given control is making.

  • ✓4-7 options as visible radio buttons, not a dropdown
  • ✓16+ options get a searchable combobox, not a long static list
  • ✓Checkbox for “applies on Save”, toggle for “applies now”, never mixed on one screen
  • ×A 20-option dropdown with no search, forcing a scroll-and-squint
Variant B of the dropdown search threshold. A plain dropdown for 8 to 15 options, a searchable combobox from 16, async search past 50. Use when: you are picking the control from the option count. Variant A, search from about 10 items, is in Dropdown Design. Both are kept on purpose.
Variant C of the option-count thresholds. A segmented control for 2 to 4 exclusive options that must stay in view (7 segments is too many); visible radios up to 5; more than 5 becomes a dropdown, because a longer radio list pushes the rest of the settings off screen. Use when: the choice sits in a settings page with other controls below it. Variant B (visible radios to 7, dropdown 8 to 15) suits a choice that has the screen to itself. All kept on purpose.
Notes
// option count decides the control, not house habit
function pickControl(optionCount) {
  if (optionCount <= 3) return 'segmented-or-radio';
  if (optionCount <= 7) return 'visible-radio-list';
  if (optionCount <= 15) return 'dropdown';
  if (optionCount <= 50) return 'searchable-combobox';
  return 'async-autocomplete';
}

16

Checkout That Feels Safe

Five quiet decisions make a payment form feel safe. The total stays in view: the order summary is sticky beside the form (the form moves, the summary does not), and the amount on the pay button matches the order total exactly (Pay $148.00 under Total due $148.00), so nothing changes at the last step; short trust lines sit under it (card details are encrypted, free returns within 30 days). The card is recognised on digit one: the brand badge appears from the first digit (4 is Visa, 5 is Mastercard, 3 is Amex); recognised first, judged later.

Red waits until the field is left: nothing turns red while the number is being typed; the field is checked on blur (Your card number is incomplete.), and once flagged it stays flagged on every keystroke until it is fixed. This is Form Validation Timing (Forms, entry 05) applied to the card field. The fastest way to pay sits on top: Apple Pay and Google Pay above every card field, one tap and no typing against six fields, with an Or pay with card divider below. Eyes go straight down: one column with every label above its field, so the eye path is one line and the label stays visible while typing; a two-column grid with placeholder-only labels makes the eye jump seven times.

  • ✓Pay button amount identical to the order total
  • ✓Card brand badge from the first digit
  • ✓Wallets above every card field
  • ✓One column, labels above fields
  • ×A card number flagged red on the first keystroke
  • ×Placeholder-only labels that vanish while typing
  • ×A two-column payment grid
HTML + JS
<!-- one column, labels above, wallets first, summary pinned -->
<form class="pay">
  <div class="wallets"><button>Apple Pay</button><button>Google Pay</button></div>
  <p class="divider">Or pay with card</p>
  <label>Card number <input id="cc" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="cc-number"></label>
  <button>Pay $148.00</button> <!-- same figure as Total due -->
</form>
<aside class="summary">Total due $148.00</aside>

.summary { position: sticky; top: 24px; } /* the form moves, the summary does not */
cc.addEventListener('input', () => {
  badge.dataset.brand = { '4': 'visa', '5': 'mastercard', '3': 'amex' }[cc.value[0]] || ''; // digit one
  if (cc.dataset.flagged) validate(cc); // once flagged, live until fixed
});
cc.addEventListener('blur', () => validate(cc)); // red waits until she leaves the field

17

Form Colour Semantics

In a settings-style form, give every colour exactly one job and the form explains itself. Labels are the primary text colour (black on light). Values and placeholders the person types are secondary grey and right aligned: grey means you type here. The tint colour (blue on iOS) means you can tap this, so date chips and pickers sit in the tint colour on a lightly tinted pill. A toggle’s on state uses the tint colour too, because active should look active; an orange or grey toggle leaves people unsure whether it is on or off.

Then group by task: the title and location together, every timing control together (all-day, starts, ends, alert), links and notes together, three grouped sections (Form Field Grouping, Forms entry 14). The failure this fixes is a form where every row is the same grey pill, so nobody can tell what is tappable, where the input goes, or which text is a label, and every row costs a small pause. Same content, but clear, logical and systematic.

  • ✓Black = label, grey = typed value, tint colour = tappable
  • ✓Toggle on state in the tint colour
  • ✓All timing controls in one group
  • ×Every row the same grey pill
  • ×A toggle colour that does not read as on or off
  • ×Tint colour on text that does nothing
CSS
.row-label { color: var(--ink); }  /* black = a label */
.row-value, .row input::placeholder { color: var(--ink-2); text-align: right; }  /* grey = you type here */
.row-chip { color: var(--tint); background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--tint) 12%, transparent); } /* tint = you can tap this */
.switch[aria-checked="true"] { background: var(--tint); }  /* active looks active */

18

Input Field Details

The small attributes on a field decide whether it is quick or a fight, especially on a phone. Width hints the answer: a postcode field is narrow and an address field is wide, so the box tells people how much to type. Every text field sets inputmode and autocomplete (email, tel, postal-code, one-time-code, name), which brings up the right keyboard and lets the browser fill in what it already knows. A maximum length exists only for a real business limit, and then a visible counter appears as the limit gets close, never a field that silently stops accepting characters. An availability check (is this username free?) runs on blur or after a 500ms pause in typing, never on every keystroke. A server error lands on its field: map every error the server returns to the field it belongs to; a generic Form invalid banner is not acceptable.

Habits to refuse. A Reset or Clear button beside Submit, where one wrong click loses everything. A CAPTCHA before anyone has tried to submit; add it only when it is needed. A sign-up that confirms the email before showing the password field, which forces an extra step for no reason. Separate first and last name fields where one full name field works. A date field that demands one fixed day and month order with no awareness of locale. A phone field with no country code. Confirm email and confirm password fields, when a show toggle does that job. A money field with no currency symbol in view. Clearing any filled field after a validation error, ever.

  • ✓Field width matched to the expected answer
  • ✓inputmode and autocomplete on every text field
  • ✓Server errors mapped to the specific field
  • ×A Reset or Clear button next to Submit
  • ×Confirm email or confirm password fields
  • ×A phone field without a country code, or a money field without its currency symbol
HTML
<!-- width hints the answer; the right keyboard and autofill on every field -->
<input name="postcode" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="postal-code" style="width:8ch">
<input name="address" autocomplete="street-address" style="width:100%">
<input name="email" type="email" inputmode="email" autocomplete="email">
<input name="phone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel">  <!-- beside a country code picker -->
<textarea name="bio" maxlength="160"></textarea>  <!-- a real limit: show 152 / 160 near the end -->

Feedback

13 patterns

What the interface says back after an action, the difference between a product that feels responsive and one that feels like a black box.

Six states, not one. Any view that fetches data or handles input needs an explicit answer for all six: Loading (see Skeleton Loading / Loading States System below), Empty (says why it’s empty and what to do next, not “no data”), Partial, Error (see Error States below), Success (a visible confirmation, not silence, see Toast Notifications / Undo UX below), and Offline. Partial and Offline are the two most commonly skipped, since neither has an obvious home the way a spinner or an error banner does. Partial covers the moment some data is in and some isn't: keep whatever already loaded on screen and slot skeleton placeholders in only for what's still coming, mark a single field that failed with an inline “Failed to load, retry” instead of erroring the whole component out, and when paginating to a next page, keep the current page visible with loading confined to the bottom rather than clearing everything first. Never blank a screen that already had real content on it, that's a step backward from where someone already was. Offline means detecting the drop (navigator.onLine plus actual failed requests, since the flag alone lies often enough not to trust on its own), surfacing a persistent banner that names the degraded mode in plain terms, queuing any mutation that can wait and retrying once the connection returns, disabling only the actions that strictly require the network, and never showing a generic error for a failure that offline status already explains.
Click both: same 900ms wait, different feel
nothing until it's done3 new leads today
3 new leads today
01

Doherty Threshold

400ms is the real deadline for a response, not a round number. Under it, attention holds and the interaction feels continuous; over it, the brain mentally checks out and starts a separate thought. The fix isn’t always a faster backend: paint a skeleton the instant a screen opens (before data has actually arrived) and apply optimistic updates for actions that are near-certain to succeed, so the perceived response lands under the threshold even when the real round trip doesn’t.

  • ✓Skeletons paint the instant a screen opens
  • ×A blank, frozen screen while data loads
JS
function openScreen() {
  renderSkeleton(); // paints in the same frame as navigation, well under 400ms
  fetchData().then(renderReal);
}

async function likePost(id) {
  setLiked(id, true); // perceived response is instant, real request happens after
  try { await api.like(id); }
  catch { setLiked(id, false); } // near-certain to succeed, so failure is the rare path
}
Severity picks the surface
⚠ Card declined, check your details and try again
Couldn't save · Retry
This action can't be completed
Contact support
02

Error States

Match the error’s surface to its actual severity: an inline message under the specific field it belongs to, a toast for something transient that will resolve itself, a page-level replacement only for a genuinely catastrophic failure, and a modal reserved for a true blocker that needs an immediate decision. A toast is the wrong surface the moment the error demands action rather than just information; it disappears on its own timer, taking the one chance to fix the problem with it. Every error needs a real way out (a retry button, a link to fix the input, a support contact), not a dead-end “OK” that just closes the dialog and leaves the underlying problem exactly where it was. Whatever someone had already typed stays exactly where it was; a validation failure or a failed save is never an excuse to clear a field and make them start over. Write the message in plain language; a raw error code or stack trace means nothing to someone who isn’t the engineer who wrote the code.

  • ✓Every error needs a real way out
  • ✓Whatever was already typed stays in the field after a failure
  • ×A dead-end “OK” with no path forward
  • ×A toast for an error that needs the user to actually do something about it
JS
function handleError(err) {
  if (err.field) return showInlineError(err.field, plainLanguage(err.code)); // one field, inline
  if (err.transient) return showToast({ msg: plainLanguage(err.code), action: { label: 'Retry', onClick: retry } });
  return showModal({ msg: plainLanguage(err.code), action: { label: 'Contact support', href: '/support' } }); // true blocker
}

const MESSAGES = { 'ERR_402': 'Payment failed, check your card details and try again.' }; // never raw codes
function plainLanguage(code) { return MESSAGES[code] ?? 'Something went wrong. Try again or contact support.'; }
Pick the pattern from what's known
known content shape
known percent complete
short, unknown-length wait
03

Loading States System

Pick the loading pattern from what’s actually known about the wait: a known content shape gets a skeleton, a known percentage gets a real progress bar, and a short wait of unknown length gets a plain spinner. A button doing its own async work is its own special case: the spinner sits inside the button, the label switches to its verb form, the button holds its own width via a minimum width so nothing shifts around it, and it disables itself for the duration so a second click can't fire the same request twice. Show nothing at all for the first ~300ms; a skeleton that flashes for a tenth of a second before real content arrives reads as a flicker, not helpful feedback. Past 2 seconds, swap a bare “Loading…” for real context, “Loading 1,247 records…” tells someone the wait has a reason. Past 10 seconds, offer a way to cancel rather than leaving them stuck watching a spinner with no exit. For anything genuinely long (past 3 seconds and climbing), show real progress wherever it's measurable, give an ETA once one is knowable, and let the operation keep running in the background with a notification when it finishes, instead of holding someone hostage on the screen that started it. For anything reversible, optimistic UI (see Feedback ’Optimistic UI’) beats a loading state entirely by skipping the wait perception altogether.

  • ✓Nothing at all under ~300ms
  • ✓Real context past 2s, a cancel option past 10s
  • ✓A button-internal spinner keeps its width and disables itself, so a second click can't double-submit
  • ×A skeleton for every fetch regardless of duration
The first moment of a wait, two variants. Variant A: show nothing for the first ~300ms of a content load, so a fast response never flickers a skeleton (this entry). Use when: data is loading into a screen or a panel. Variant B: acknowledge within 100ms, with the pressed state and a spinner inside the button from the moment of the press (Interactive State and Affordance, Interaction entry 24). Use when: the person just clicked or tapped something. Both are kept on purpose; one action often needs both, B on the button and A on the panel it fills.
JS
function withLoadingState(promise, { onSlow, delayMs = 300 }) {
  const timer = setTimeout(onSlow, delayMs); // nothing shown before this fires
  return promise.finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}

// pick the pattern by what's actually known about the wait
function pickLoader({ knownShape, knownPercent }) {
  if (knownPercent) return 'progress-bar';
  if (knownShape) return 'skeleton';
  return 'spinner'; // short, unknown-length wait
}
Four surfaces, one severity ladder

04

Notification System

A notification system is really four distinct surfaces (toast, banner, modal, badge), and severity is what should pick which one fires, not habit or whichever component was easiest to reach for. Toasts auto-dismiss and carry undo for low-stakes, reversible events; modals are reserved for things that genuinely block progress. Low-priority toasts need to stack and breathe with a visible gap between them rather than overlapping, and routing everything to the loudest available surface trains people to ignore all of them equally.

Badges. A badge carries two different signals that need different treatment. A count is an action: it says how many, asks you to act now, and changes with each new item. A status dot is a condition: it says which state, asks for nothing, and reads green for online and red for act now. Never put both on one row, since a dot says something changed, a number says how much, and both together is noise. Cap the count so the width is bounded (one unread shows a single dot or number, 200 shows 99+, whereas an uncapped 661 grows the pill and reflows the nav), and pin the badge to the icon’s top corner so the icon never moves whether it shows one digit or three.

A badge clears the second the view is opened; one that lingers after you have looked trains people to ignore every badge. When the count climbs it ticks up and never resets to zero on screen, because that flash reads as a bug. And badge the decision, not everything: for example, badging Messages, Mentions, Product updates, Promotions and System makes the colour meaningless, while badging only Mentions keeps the signal.

  • ✓Toasts auto-dismiss with undo; modals for true blockers
  • ✓Badge counts cap at 99+, width bounded so a real spike can’t break the layout
  • ✓Badge pinned to the icon’s top corner, so the icon never moves
  • ✓One signal per row: a count or a status dot, never both
  • ✓The badge clears the moment the view opens; the count ticks up and never blinks to zero
  • ✓Only things that need a decision get a badge
  • ×Routing everything to the loudest surface
  • ×Badging every category, until the colour means nothing
  • ×A badge that lingers after the user has looked
JS
function notify({ severity, message, undo }) {
  if (severity === 'low') return pushToast({ message, undo, autoDismiss: 4000 }); // stacks, breathes
  if (severity === 'medium') return showBanner({ message }); // persistent until dismissed
  if (severity === 'blocking') return showModal({ message }); // only true blockers get here
  bumpBadge(); // passive count, no interruption at all
}
JS + CSS: badge rules
const label = (n) => (n > 99 ? '99+' : String(n)); // capped, so the width is bounded (200 shows 99+, never 661)

function setBadge(el, n) {
  el.textContent = label(n); // when the count climbs it ticks up: never reset to 0 on screen and back
  el.hidden = n === 0;
}
function openInbox() { markAllRead(); setBadge(bell, 0); } // open it, clear it: the second the view opens

.bell   { position: relative; }
.badge  { position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0; transform: translate(50%, -50%); overflow: hidden; } /* pinned to the icon's top corner: the icon never moves */
.status-dot { border-radius: 50%; } /* a condition, not a count: green = online, red = act now */
/* one signal per row: render a .badge or a .status-dot, never both; badge only what needs a decision */
Compare the two, click both
Optimistic, safe (a count)
Pessimistic, correct (a save)
05

Optimistic UI

Update the interface the instant someone acts, sync the real request in the background, and roll back cleanly if it fails. The perceived latency drops to zero even though the network call still takes its normal time. This is reserved for reversible, low-stakes actions where a rollback costs nothing (a like, a follow, an inline edit); trust the success case and design failure as the rare exception rather than the default assumption. Never apply it to a payment or anything else unsafe to silently reverse.

  • ✓Reserved for reversible, low-stakes actions
  • ×Optimistic payments or anything unsafe to undo
JS
async function optimisticUpdate(id, nextState, apiCall) {
  const previous = getState(id);
  setState(id, nextState); // applied instantly, before the request even starts
  try {
    await apiCall();
  } catch {
    setState(id, previous); // clean rollback, only reachable for reversible actions
    notify({ severity: 'low', message: 'Update failed, reverted.' });
  }
}

Matches the loaded content's real dimensions, nothing jumps
06

Skeleton Loading

A skeleton previews the real content’s shape (card outlines, text-line bars) so the brain starts parsing the layout before the actual data has arrived, which measurably reduces the perceived wait versus a blank screen or spinner. It needs to animate (a shimmer sweep) and match the real content’s dimensions closely, or the layout visibly jumps the moment data replaces it. Skip a loading state entirely for an action just performed by the same user (like a submit that immediately shows its own result); they already know it’s working.

  • ✓Animate the shimmer, match real dimensions
  • ×A skeleton that jumps to a different layout on load
CSS
.skeleton {
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--sk-base) 25%, var(--sk-shine) 50%, var(--sk-base) 75%);
  background-size: 200% 100%;
  animation: shimmer 1.4s ease-in-out infinite;
  border-radius: 6px;
}
@keyframes shimmer { to { background-position: -200% 0; } }

/* match the REAL element's exact dimensions so nothing jumps on swap */
.skeleton-avatar { width: 40px; height: 40px; border-radius: 50%; }
.skeleton-title  { width: 60%; height: 16px; margin-bottom: 8px; }
.skeleton-line   { width: 100%; height: 12px; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .skeleton { animation: none; opacity: .6; } }
Fire a toast, bottom-right
✓ Changes saved
07

Toast Notifications

Position toasts deliberately (bottom-right on desktop, a top-edge banner on mobile) and never dead-centre over active content, where they block exactly what someone is trying to look at. Match the dismiss timing to severity: a routine confirmation clears in a few seconds, a warning holds longer or waits for a manual dismiss. Cap the visible stack at three and pause the auto-dismiss timer on hover so a toast doesn’t vanish mid-read, and always pair colour with an icon; colour alone is the same accessibility failure it is everywhere else in this document. The right confirmation still depends on what just happened. An inline edit gets a quiet green flash plus a checkmark on the field itself for about 1.5 seconds, no toast needed. A form submit that keeps someone on the same page gets a toast plus a visible change in the data they're looking at. A form submit that navigates somewhere new shows the confirmation as context on the destination itself, “Created John Smith” at the top of his new record, rather than a toast that's already gone by the time the new page renders. A batch action gets a plain summary count, “Suspended 12 users”, not a silent redirect that leaves someone guessing whether it worked.

  • ✓Cap the stack at 3, pause on hover
  • ✓Confirmation matches the action: inline flash, toast, destination context, or a batch summary count
  • ×Colour-only type signalling, no icon
  • ×Silent success, leaving someone to guess whether it actually worked
JS
const queue = [];
function pushToast(toast) {
  queue.push({ ...toast, id: crypto.randomUUID() });
  if (queue.length > 3) queue.shift(); // stack capped at 3
  render();
}

toastEl.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => clearTimeout(toastEl._timer)); // pause on hover
toastEl.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => {
  toastEl._timer = setTimeout(() => dismiss(toastEl), toastEl.dataset.severity === 'warning' ? 6000 : 3000);
});
Delete a row, then undo it
Follow-up: Daniel Hoffmann
Follow-up: Kavita Nandan
Deleted
08

Undo UX

Undo beats a confirmation dialog for most destructive actions: act immediately with zero friction, then offer a real second chance via a toast instead of asking “are you sure?” before anything has even happened, a question people click through without reading anyway. Soft-delete under the hood with a genuine recovery window (not an instant hard-delete dressed up with an undo button that does nothing), and show a visible countdown on the toast so the window’s urgency is honest rather than a guess.

  • ✓Soft-delete with a real recovery window
  • ×Blocking every delete behind a confirm nobody reads
Undo toast duration, two variants. Variant A: about 4 seconds for a reversible, low-stakes change such as a notification setting (Success States, entry 12). Use when: the change is trivial to redo by hand. Variant B: 5 to 10 seconds, longer for anything destructive, with the countdown visible. Use when: the undo recovers something deleted or sent. Both are kept on purpose.
JS
function deleteWithUndo(item) {
  softDelete(item.id); // happens immediately, no "are you sure" dialog
  const deadline = Date.now() + 5000;
  pushToast({
    message: `Deleted "${item.title}"`,
    countdown: deadline, // toast renders a live countdown against this
    action: { label: 'Undo', onClick: () => restore(item.id) },
    onExpire: () => hardDelete(item.id), // only now is it actually gone
  });
}

09

Zeigarnik Effect

The mind keeps an unfinished task active in working memory and drops a finished one almost instantly. A visibly incomplete progress bar pulls attention back in a way a completed one never does. A profile-completeness meter with one deliberate box left unchecked (“Add a photo”) exploits exactly this to bring someone back to finish it. The open loop has to tie to an outcome the person actually wants, not a made-up metric; manufacturing progress nobody asked to track just reads as manipulative busywork.

  • ✓One deliberate box left unchecked in onboarding
  • ×Manufacturing progress nobody asked to track
JS
const profileSteps = [
  { key: 'name', done: true },
  { key: 'avatar', done: false }, // deliberately left open, pulls the user back
  { key: 'bio', done: true },
];
const pct = Math.round((profileSteps.filter(s => s.done).length / profileSteps.length) * 100);
// "Profile 90% complete, add a photo to finish" ties the open loop to a real, wanted outcome
Same “delete”, four tiers of friction

High, typed confirm

10

Destructive Action Risk Tiers

Not every destructive action deserves the same friction, and matching friction to actual consequence is what makes the friction mean something instead of training people to click through it. Four tiers, escalating with what’s actually at stake. Low risk, with a clear undo path (delete a draft, remove a filter), gets a single click plus a toast with undo, no modal at all (see Undo UX above). Medium risk, with some recovery path (delete a project, remove a teammate), gets a confirmation modal with the destructive button styled red and labelled with the verb (see Destructive Actions in Interaction above for the hold-to-confirm mechanic that pairs with this tier). High risk, with real consequences (delete a client’s account, wipe a dataset), escalates to a modal that requires typing the resource’s name or the word DELETE before the button activates at all. Critical risk that genuinely can’t be recovered (close an account, revoke every API key) adds a password or 2FA re-entry on top of the typed confirmation. Whatever the tier, focus defaults to Cancel, never to the destructive button itself.

  • ✓Friction escalates with actual consequence, not with how severe the action feels
  • ✓Confirmation dialog focus defaults to Cancel, never the destructive button
  • ×One “are you sure?” modal used identically for a draft delete and an account close
JS
// tier -> UI treatment
const DESTRUCTIVE_TIERS = {
  low:      { ui: 'toast+undo',      confirm: false },
  medium:   { ui: 'modal',            confirm: 'click' },
  high:     { ui: 'modal-typed',      confirm: 'type-resource-name' },
  critical: { ui: 'modal-typed+2fa',  confirm: 'type-resource-name+reauth' },
};

function confirmDialog(tier, resourceName) {
  return {
    defaultFocus: 'cancel', // every tier, never the destructive button
    requiresTyping: (tier === 'high' || tier === 'critical') ? resourceName : null,
    requiresReauth: tier === 'critical',
  };
}
Click both: one confirms on the same frame, one makes you wait
Wrong: a 480ms spinner before the check
demo_key_4f9a2c81
Right: the check lands on the same frame
demo_key_4f9a2c81
11

Copy to Clipboard

A copy button changes nothing on screen by itself, so it has to prove it worked. 1. Flip instantly. The copy icon becomes a check on the same frame the copy fires, with no spinner and no delay; a 480ms spinner feels broken next to a 0ms flip. 2. Reset after two seconds. Hold the check for about two seconds, then fade back to the copy icon; if it stays stuck, the second copy gives no signal at all. 3. Copy the raw value. Copy the plain string, not the formatted span with its line breaks and hidden zero-width characters, which break when pasted into a terminal (the demo shows a parse error against “authenticated”). 4. Say it out loud. A silent icon change is invisible to a screen reader, so announce “Copied” through a polite aria-live region. 5. Fall back, don’t lie. On an insecure origin (for example plain http) the modern clipboard call fails, so try navigator.clipboard.writeText, catch the failure, fall back to the older execCommand copy, and show an honest message if both are blocked. A silent button lies.

  • ✓The icon flips to a check on the same frame the copy fires, no spinner
  • ✓The check holds for about 2 seconds, then fades back to the copy icon
  • ✓Copy the raw string, never the formatted span
  • ✓Announce “Copied” through a polite aria-live region
  • ✓Try the modern call, catch, fall back to execCommand, and show an honest message if both are blocked
  • ×A spinner or delay between the click and the confirmation
  • ×A check that never resets, so the second copy gives no signal
  • ×A silent failure, or a check shown when nothing was copied
Two accuracy notes. On an insecure origin the modern clipboard API is usually unavailable altogether (navigator.clipboard is undefined) rather than failing silently, so check for it before calling it. And document.execCommand('copy') is officially deprecated though still widely supported, so treat the fallback as pragmatic, not ideal. Related entries: Toast Notifications, Undo UX and Interactive State & Affordance.
JS
async function copyRaw(btn, live) {
  const raw = btn.dataset.copy;           // the plain string, never the formatted span's innerText (line breaks, zero-width characters)
  const ok = await writeClipboard(raw); // no spinner state exists between the click and the check
  if (!ok) { live.textContent = 'Could not copy. Select the text and press Ctrl+C.'; return; } // an honest message, not a lying check
  btn.classList.add('copied');          // copy icon becomes a check, instantly
  live.textContent = 'Copied';           // polite aria-live region: screen readers announce it
  setTimeout(() => { btn.classList.remove('copied'); live.textContent = ''; }, 2000); // reset after about 2 seconds, fade back
}

async function writeClipboard(text) {
  try { await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text); return true; } // navigator.clipboard is undefined on insecure origins, so this throws
  catch (_) {
    const ta = Object.assign(document.createElement('textarea'), { value: text });
    document.body.appendChild(ta); ta.select();
    const ok = document.execCommand('copy'); // deprecated but still widely supported: pragmatic, not ideal
    ta.remove();
    return ok; // false = both paths blocked, so tell the user
  }
}
<!-- <div id="copy-live" aria-live="polite"></div>  the live region must already exist in the DOM -->

12

Success States

A done screen is not a dead end, and five decisions keep the person moving. Say what happened: what, who and when, with the specifics (Invoice sent to Northwind Labs, INV-2051, EUR 2,400, due 12 Oct, sent just now) instead of Success! Your action was completed; specifics are the proof it worked, and a vague success feels like a maybe. Offer the next action: one primary next step and one way back (View invoice, Send another, Back to invoices); a check mark with no button is a dead end, and the person closes the tab right there.

Dismissal follows stakes: a reversible, low-stakes change (notification settings) gets a toast with Undo that leaves after about 4 seconds; money gets a page that stays, with the plan, amount, card, date, a downloadable receipt and a copy by email, because nobody screenshots a toast. Leave one open loop: one thread to pull, such as tracking the payment (sent, opened, paid, notify me when paid), sharing the report, or inviting teammates; a finished task with a thread to pull brings people back (Zeigarnik Effect, Feedback entry 09). Celebrate the rare win: confetti is for milestones such as the first invoice paid, never every save; rare joy lands, constant joy is noise (Peak-End Rule, Interaction entry 18).

  • ✓What, who and when, with real specifics
  • ✓One primary next action and one way back
  • ✓Reversible = toast with Undo; money = a page with a receipt
  • ✓Confetti for milestones only
  • ×Success! with an OK button and nothing else
  • ×A payment confirmed only by a toast
  • ×Confetti on every save
JS
// success = what + who + when, one primary next step, one way back
function onDone(r) {
  if (r.reversible && !r.money) toast(`${r.what} saved`, { action: 'Undo', ms: 4000 }); // low stakes
  else showPage('receipt', r); // money: a page that stays, receipt plus email
  if (r.milestone) confetti(); // first invoice paid, never every save
}
One component, all six states designed
Loading
EmptyNo invoices yetCreate
Partial1 failed, Retry
ErrorCouldn’t load. Retry
Success✓ Saved just now
OfflineSaved on this device
13

Six Data States

Anything that fetches data, accepts input or does async work has six states, and each one is designed rather than left to whatever the happy path happens to render. Loading shows a skeleton that matches the final layout, or a progress indicator with intent (Loading States System, entry 03). Empty explains why and offers the next action (Empty States, Content entry 01). Partial shows what did load and marks what did not. Error says what happened and offers a way out (Error States, entry 02). Success is a visible confirmation, never just the absence of an error (Success States, entry 12). Offline is a degraded mode with an explanation.

Partial is the most skipped state. When some items have loaded and more are coming, show the loaded items with skeleton placeholders for the rest. When one field or panel fails, mark only that spot with Failed to load, Retry, rather than turning the whole component into an error. When the next page is loading, keep the current page visible and show the loader at the bottom. Never blank the screen on a partial failure; that throws away data the person already had.

Offline, at minimum. Detect it (navigator.onLine plus failed requests). Say so in a persistent banner (Offline, your changes are saved on this device). Queue changes and replay them on reconnect where possible (Autosave, Forms entry 01). Disable the actions that strictly need the network, and raise no errors for failures that being offline already explains. If the product genuinely cannot work offline, say so the first time it happens rather than failing silently. Before calling a data component done, tick all six states; any unticked one is a gap to fix or to name out loud.

  • ✓All six states handled: loading, empty, partial, error, success, offline
  • ✓A partial failure marks one spot and keeps everything else on screen
  • ✓A persistent offline banner, with changes queued for reconnect
  • ×A component that only renders the happy path
  • ×Blanking the screen when one request out of five fails
  • ×A wall of network errors for something being offline already explains
JSX
// all six states, in the order they are checked
if (offline && !data)  return <OfflineState onRetry={refetch} />;   // degraded mode, explained
if (isLoading)         return <ListSkeleton rows={5} />;           // same shape as the real list
if (isError)           return <ErrorState title="We couldn't load invoices" onRetry={refetch} />;
if (data.length === 0) return <EmptyState action="Create your first invoice" />;
return (<>
  {offline && <Banner>Offline, your changes are saved on this device</Banner>}
  <List items={data} failed={failedIds} />  {/* partial: a failed row shows Retry inline */}
</>);

Visual

32 patterns

The layer people notice consciously least and judge most: colour, depth, spacing, and the perceptual rules underneath them.

Radius scales with element size
4px · badge
8px · button
12px · card
16px · modal
01

Border Radius

Nested corners follow real math: a card with 12px radius and 8px padding needs an inner element radius of exactly 4px (outer minus padding), or the inner corner reads as visually off even though nobody can say why. Pick one radius scale for the whole system (4/8/12/16, or similar) instead of eyeballing a number per component, and scale the radius up with element size; a tiny badge and a full page card at the same 8px radius look proportionally wrong on the smaller one. Radius is also a brand lever: sharp corners read technical/serious, generous rounding reads friendly/approachable, so pick deliberately.

The full checklist has six rules. Nested: inner radius equals outer radius minus padding (a 12px card with 8px padding gets a 4px inner corner), so nested corners share one centre; otherwise the inner corner bulges. Scale: size sets the radius (for example small 4, medium 8, large 16, which are sample values), not 8px on everything; a chip and a modal do not share a corner. Pill: full radius is a shape, not a number, so use 9999px only on a single-line element such as a chip, avatar or toggle, never on a multi-line card. Edges: an element that touches an edge has no corner there, so a bottom sheet flush to the screen edge gets its top corners rounded and its bottom corners at zero. Ring: a selection ring drawn as its own box sits outside the element, so ring radius equals the inner radius plus the gap (8 inside and a 2px gap gives 10 out); if the corners pinch, flip the formula. Images: an edge-to-edge image in a rounded card is clipped by the card (overflow: hidden) so square image corners do not poke through; for an inset image, subtract the padding and apply the same nested rule.

  • ✓Scale radius with element size
  • ✓Focus ring radius matches the element’s own radius
  • ✓Image corners clipped to their container’s radius, not left square
  • ✓Pill radius (9999px) only on single-line shapes such as a chip, avatar or toggle
  • ✓No rounded corner where an element touches an edge: a flush bottom sheet keeps only its top corners
  • ✓A selection ring drawn as its own box gets the element’s radius plus the gap (8 inside, 10 out for a 2px gap)
  • ×Random per-component radius values
  • ×9999px on a multi-line card
CSS
:root {
  --radius-sm: 4px;  --radius-md: 8px;  --radius-lg: 12px;  --radius-xl: 16px;
}
.badge  { border-radius: var(--radius-sm); }
.button { border-radius: var(--radius-md); }
.card   { border-radius: var(--radius-lg); padding: 16px; }
/* nested corner math: outer radius − padding = correct inner radius */
.card .card-inner { border-radius: calc(var(--radius-lg) - 16px); } /* = -4px → clamp to 0 */
.card .card-inner-tight { padding: 8px; border-radius: calc(var(--radius-lg) - 8px); } /* = 4px, correct */

.chip, .avatar, .toggle { border-radius: 9999px; } /* pill: single-line shapes only, never a multi-line card */
.sheet { border-radius: var(--radius-xl) var(--radius-xl) 0 0; } /* flush to the screen edge: no corner where it touches */
.selectable { padding: 2px; } /* the gap between the element and its ring */
.selectable .ring { border-radius: calc(var(--radius-md) + 2px); } /* ring = inner radius (8) + gap (2) = 10; if the corners pinch, flip the formula */
.card { overflow: hidden; } /* edge-to-edge image: the card clips it, so square image corners never poke through */
.card .inset-img { margin: 8px; border-radius: calc(var(--radius-lg) - 8px); } /* inset image: subtract the padding, same nested rule */
Same data, two y-axes
Truncated axis, looks huge
Zero-based, the true 2% gap
02

Charts That Lie

Every bar chart’s y-axis starts at zero. Truncating it to, say, 90-100 turns a genuinely small 2% change into a bar that looks three times taller than its neighbour, which is a factual misrepresentation even if every number on the chart is technically correct. Match the chart type to the actual question being asked (trend over time is a line, comparison across categories is a bar, part-of-whole is rarely a pie), and title the chart with the takeaway itself, not the bare metric name. Skip gridlines, 3D extrusion, or decorative elements that encode no real data; they add visual noise without adding information.

  • ✓Chart type matched to the actual question
  • ×Gridlines/3D that encode no real data
JS: chart config
const chartConfig = {
  type: 'bar',
  scales: { y: { beginAtZero: true } }, // non-negotiable, truncation misrepresents the data
  plugins: {
    title: { text: 'Signups grew 34% after the pricing change' }, // the takeaway, not "Signups"
    legend: { display: false }, // only shown when there's more than one series
  },
  elements: { bar: { borderWidth: 0 } }, // no 3D bevel, no decorative gridlines
};
Real pairs, checked against WCAG AA
Body text on card8.1:1 PASS
Muted caption grey2.3:1 FAIL
03

Color Accessibility

Contrast is always a ratio between a colour and whatever sits directly behind it; there’s no such thing as an accessible colour in isolation. Check every real foreground/background pair against WCAG (4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and UI components), and give every colour-coded cue a second signal (an icon, a pattern, a text label) so a red/green status distinction doesn’t collapse entirely for a colour-blind user. The usual failure spot is a “decorative” muted grey caption that nobody thought to check, not the obvious high-stakes error text.

  • ✓Second signal (icon/pattern) with every colour cue
  • ×Red-vs-green as the only signal
JS
function contrastRatio(fg, bg) { /* same relative-luminance formula as Color Picker UX above */ }

const pairs = [
  { name: 'caption grey on card', fg: '#9AA3AF', bg: '#FFFFFF' }, // the usual missed spot
  { name: 'error text', fg: '#C0392B', bg: '#FFFFFF' },
];
pairs.forEach(p => {
  const ratio = contrastRatio(p.fg, p.bg);
  console.log(`${p.name}: ${ratio.toFixed(2)}:1, ${ratio >= 4.5 ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL'} AA body`);
});
// status dot: colour is never the only signal
// <span class="status status-error">⚠ Failed</span>, icon + text label alongside colour
Near-black vs. pure black
#121212
correct base
#000000
harsh halation
surface+1
elevation via lightness
04

Dark Mode

Dark mode is not black mode. Build the base surface on a near-black like #121212, never pure #000, which creates harsh halation against any bright element and looks cheap on OLED. Desaturate accent colours by roughly 20% in dark mode, since a saturated colour that looks right on white can vibrate uncomfortably against near-black. Use layered, progressively lighter surfaces to signal elevation instead of shadows (which barely read on a dark ground), and build text hierarchy through opacity tiers on a single white rather than several different hardcoded greys.

Six rules, in full. Near black, not black: pure black saves OLED battery but kills depth, since nothing can sit lower than black, so start near black (for example a page at #0B0D10, with the card and chip lighter). Lightness is elevation: shadows die on dark, so raise surfaces by making them lighter, with page, card, menu and modal each one step lighter. Three tiers of white: never pure white text; primary at about 87%, secondary at about 60% and disabled at about 38%, one colour with three alphas. Calm the accent: a saturated brand blue glows past its edges on dark, so keep the hue but lighten and desaturate it. Alpha hairlines: edges need a 1px line of white at about 8% alpha rather than a fixed grey, because it adapts as the surface gets lighter. Dim the photos: bright images pull the eye on a dim page, so lower their brightness to about 90%, and give illustrations a redrawn dark variant rather than a filter.

  • ✓Layered surfaces signal elevation
  • ✓Text tiers on one white: about 87% primary, 60% secondary, 38% disabled
  • ✓Edges as a 1px white line at about 8% alpha, not a fixed grey
  • ✓Photos dimmed to about 90% brightness; illustrations redrawn as a dark variant, not filtered
  • ×Pure white body text glaring on dark
  • ×A saturated brand colour left unchanged on dark, glowing past its edges
Real trade-off, not a free upgrade: near-black elevation surfaces cost more battery on OLED than true black, and several of the lighter "elevated" surface tones can quietly fail WCAG contrast if not checked; a low-contrast button on a near-black surface is the classic miss. Run every elevated surface + text pair through the Color Accessibility check above before shipping; don't assume "near-black" is automatically accessible just because it isn't pure black. Two fair objections: saving battery can matter more than depth, and most of these techniques lower contrast; and an accent desaturated too far looks disabled. Treat the 87, 60 and 38 percent tiers, the 8% alpha hairline and the 90% photo brightness as sensible defaults to check, not rules, and keep the contrast check above.
CSS
:root[data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg: #121212; /* near-black, never pure #000 */
  --surface-1: #1E1E1E; --surface-2: #262626; --surface-3: #2E2E2E; /* elevation via lightness, not shadow */
  --text-high: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.87); /* opacity tiers, not separate hex greys */
  --text-med:  rgb(255 255 255 / 0.60);
  --text-low:  rgb(255 255 255 / 0.38);
  --accent: oklch(70% 0.12 175); /* ~20% less saturated than the light-mode accent */
  --border: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.08); /* alpha hairline: adapts as the surface gets lighter, unlike a fixed grey */
}
img, video { filter: brightness(0.9); } /* dim photos to about 90%; give illustrations a redrawn dark variant instead of a filter */
Hover to feel the lift
Hover me
Hover me
Hover me
05

Depth Layers

Three CSS levers create real perceived depth without a visual redesign: layered box-shadows (a tight contact shadow plus a soft ambient one), a subtle parallax speed differential between background and foreground on scroll, and a small hover z-lift. Stack a tight shadow with a wider ambient one rather than one flat blur value; that combination is what makes an element read as physically raised. Keep hover lifts subtle: a few pixels of translateY and roughly 3% scale reads as responsive; push either further and it starts to feel gimmicky rather than tactile.

  • ✓Stack tight + mid + ambient shadows
  • ×Parallax/scale pushed far enough to distract
CSS
.elevated {
  box-shadow:
    0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / .08),   /* tight contact shadow */
    0 4px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / .06),   /* mid */
    0 12px 24px rgb(0 0 0 / .05); /* soft ambient */
  transition: transform 200ms ease, box-shadow 200ms ease;
}
.elevated:hover {
  transform: translateY(-2px) scale(1.03); /* subtle: a few px, ~3% */
  box-shadow: 0 2px 4px rgb(0 0 0 / .1), 0 8px 16px rgb(0 0 0 / .08), 0 20px 32px rgb(0 0 0 / .06);
}
.parallax-bg { transform: translateY(calc(var(--scroll-y) * 0.3px)); } /* moves slower than foreground */
Numbered colour scale + 4px spacing scale
4 · 8 · 12 · 16 · 24
06

Design System Kit

Semantic tokens like --brand or --error survive a rebrand or a dark-mode pass because the name describes the role, not the literal colour behind it; hardcoded hex scattered across components has to be found and changed one at a time. Build a numbered colour scale (50 through 900) for every hue rather than a handful of arbitrary shades, and a 4px spacing scale so every gap in the product traces back to one shared rhythm. Define components as combinations of variant/size/state rather than one-off classes per screen.

  • ✓Numbered colour scale + 4px spacing scale
  • ×Hardcoded hex and eyeballed gaps
CSS
:root {
  --blue-50: #EFF2FB; --blue-500: #3B5BDB; --blue-900: #0F1B3E; /* numbered scale, not one-off hex */
  --space-1: 4px; --space-2: 8px; --space-3: 12px; --space-4: 16px; --space-6: 24px; /* 4px rhythm */
  --brand: var(--blue-500); --error: #C0392B; --success: #27AE60; /* semantic layer on top */
}
/* component = variant + size + state, not a new class per screen */
.btn[data-variant="primary"][data-size="md"] { background: var(--brand); padding: var(--space-2) var(--space-4); }
.btn[data-variant="primary"]:disabled { background: var(--blue-50); color: var(--blue-500); }

→
color-primary
