Motion

6 patterns

The smallest category, but the one where a wrong number is felt by everyone even when nobody can name what’s off.

Staggered entrance, ~50ms apart
Follow-up: Daniel Hoffmann
Follow-up: Kavita Nandan
Follow-up: Maya Chen
01

Animation Timing

An element entering the screen lands best at 200-300ms with an ease-out curve, long enough to read as deliberate motion, short enough not to feel sluggish. Exits should run noticeably faster than their entrance, around 150ms, because something leaving the screen doesn’t need to earn the same attention something new arriving does. Tap/click feedback (a button’s pressed state) needs to register in under 100ms without exception; anything slower reads as lag, not animation. When staggering a list of items into view, roughly 50ms between each item is enough to read as a cascade rather than a delay. A hover response specifically should register around 60ms, and no interaction transition in a dense productivity UI should run past ~150ms or use an overshoot/bounce easing curve. A snappy, no-overshoot response is what makes a tool feel instantly answering rather than animating at you.

To stagger a list in one rule, instead of a hand-set delay on every item, use the CSS function sibling-index(), which returns an element’s position among its siblings: animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 100ms) with the keyframes unchanged. It works for a list of any length, including items added later, with no per-item CSS or JavaScript. It starts at 1, so use calc((sibling-index() - 1) * 50ms) when the first item should have no delay. Support is Chrome and Edge 138 and Safari 26.x, with Firefox still missing as of mid-2026, so keep the --i variable as the fallback.

  • ✓Tap feedback under 100ms, always
  • ✓~60ms hover response, no overshoot/bounce easing in dense UI
  • ✓Stagger with sibling-index() where supported, the --i variable as the fallback
  • ×Symmetric in/out timing that drags
  • ×A 600ms interface animation: it reads as broken past the 150 to 250ms band
Variants held here. A: entrances land at 200 to 300ms with ease-out. Use when: an element is entering the screen. B: nothing in a dense productivity UI runs past about 150ms, and exits run around 150ms. Use when: the screen is a dense productivity UI, which is this entry’s own wording (Dropdown Design’s 150ms open is variant B). C: interface motion stays in a 150 to 250ms band with 250ms as the shared ceiling. Use when: you want one number for general interface motion. All three are kept on purpose.
CSS
:root {
  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
  --dur-tap: 80ms;    /* feedback, never slower than this */
  --dur-enter: 250ms; /* entrances */
  --dur-exit: 150ms;  /* exits run faster than entrances */
}
.btn:active { transform: scale(.97); transition: transform var(--dur-tap) ease-out; }
.modal-enter { animation: fade-up var(--dur-enter) var(--ease-out); }
.modal-exit  { animation: fade-down var(--dur-exit) ease-in; } /* faster than the enter */

.list-item { animation: fade-up 250ms var(--ease-out) backwards; }
.list-item:nth-child(n) { animation-delay: calc(var(--i, 0) * 50ms); } /* ~50ms stagger */

/* CSS-native stagger where supported: no per-item variable, and it works for items added later */
/* sibling-index() starts at 1, so subtract 1 when the first item should have no delay */
@supports (width: calc(sibling-index() * 1px)) {
  .list-item:nth-child(n) { animation-delay: calc((sibling-index() - 1) * 50ms); }
}
/* a shorter version: li { animation: in .4s backwards; animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 100ms); }
   @keyframes in { from { opacity: 0; translate: -20px } } ; the --i rule above stays as the fallback */
Hover: card lifts, image scales inside its frame
Neighbours never shift, only this card and its image move
02

Card Hover Anatomy

Lift the card itself with real physical weight (roughly 8px of translateY over about 200ms) and animate what’s inside the card (an image scaling up, actions fading in), never the card’s own outer footprint, which would shove neighbouring cards around in a grid. Stagger any actions that reveal on hover roughly 60ms apart so they cascade in rather than popping simultaneously, and scale an inner image inside an overflow: hidden frame so the zoom stays contained within the card’s fixed bounds.

  • ✓Scale the image inside an overflow-hidden frame
  • ×Scaling the whole card, shifting neighbours
CSS
.card { transition: transform 200ms var(--ease-out), box-shadow 200ms; }
.card:hover { transform: translateY(-8px); } /* lifts the card, doesn't resize its footprint */

.card-image-frame { overflow: hidden; border-radius: 8px 8px 0 0; } /* contains the zoom */
.card-image-frame img { transition: transform 300ms var(--ease-out); }
.card:hover .card-image-frame img { transform: scale(1.08); } /* image scales, card footprint doesn't */

.card-actions { display: flex; gap: 8px; }
.card-actions > * { transition: opacity 150ms, transform 150ms; }
.card-actions > *:nth-child(1) { transition-delay: 0ms; }
.card-actions > *:nth-child(2) { transition-delay: 60ms; } /* ~60ms stagger */
Same distance, three curves
linear
ease-out (default)
spring (confirmations)
03

Easing Curves

The shape of an easing curve is what the eye actually perceives, even holding distance and total duration constant. Linear motion at constant speed reads as robotic because almost nothing in the physical world moves that way. Ease-out (fast start, gentle stop) is the right default for anything entering the screen, since it mimics how a real object decelerates as it arrives. A small spring overshoot (slightly past the resting position before settling back) adds a satisfying, tactile confirmation feel to success states and toggles. Linear easing is really only appropriate for something that has no start or stop of its own, like a continuously looping spinner.

  • ✓Ease-out as the default for anything entering
  • ×Linear easing on UI that starts and stops
  • ×A spring or bounce on a dropdown or menu (fun once, tiring by the tenth time)
CSS
:root {
  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);      /* default for anything entering */
  --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1);  /* for state changes with no clear start/end */
  --ease-spring: cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); /* slight overshoot, confirmations */
}
.toast-enter { animation: slide-up 250ms var(--ease-out); }
.success-check { animation: pop 400ms var(--ease-spring); } /* overshoots then settles */
.spinner { animation: spin 900ms linear infinite; } /* linear is correct, no start/stop */
Scroll inside the box
scroll down ↓
Revealed by IntersectionObserver as it enters view, the same idea CSS animation-timeline: view() does natively, zero JS
keep scrolling
04

Scroll-Driven Animations

Native CSS animation-timeline: scroll() turns the scrollbar itself into an animation controller with zero JavaScript and zero scroll-listener jank. The browser drives the animation progress directly from scroll position on its own compositor thread. The related view() timeline animates an element specifically as it enters and exits the viewport, ideal for scroll-triggered reveals. Pair either with position: sticky for effects like a header that shrinks as it pins to the top. A hand-rolled scroll-listener re-implementation of this is strictly worse: it runs on the main thread and is the classic source of janky parallax.

  • ✓view() to animate elements as they enter
  • ×Hand-rolled scroll-listener parallax
CSS
@keyframes fade-in-up { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(24px); } to { opacity: 1; transform: none; } }

.reveal-on-scroll {
  animation: fade-in-up linear both;
  animation-timeline: view(); /* progress driven by the element entering the viewport */
  animation-range: entry 0% cover 30%; /* fully in by 30% scrolled into view */
}

.shrinking-header {
  position: sticky; top: 0;
  animation: shrink-header linear both;
  animation-timeline: scroll(); /* driven by the page's own scroll position, zero JS */
}
@keyframes shrink-header { to { padding-block: 8px; font-size: 14px; } }
/* @supports fallback: browsers without support just render the resting (non-shrunk) state */
Replay: origin at the trigger, then width against scaleX
RenameDuplicateDelete
origin: center, so it appears from nowhere
RenameDuplicateDelete
origin: top left, so it grows from the trigger
width: 12% to 100% (relayout every frame)
transform: scaleX(0.12 to 1) (compositor only, looks identical)
Scale is exaggerated so the origin is visible. With the OS reduced-motion setting on, this page skips the replay animations.
05

Motion That Stays Cheap

Interface motion goes wrong in six ways, and the first three are already covered by Animation Timing and Easing Curves: a 600ms animation reads as broken, so keep interface motion in the 150 to 250ms band; linear easing looks mechanical, so use ease-out (fast off the mark, gentle at the end); and a spring on a dropdown is fun once and tiring by the tenth time, so save the bounce for a celebration. The other three are here. 4. Origin. Set transform-origin so a menu grows out of the thing that opened it, instead of fading in from nowhere. 5. Reduced motion. If the user turned the setting on, give them a fade and never a flight: an @media (prefers-reduced-motion) rule that swaps a 300px move for an opacity fade. 6. The jank. Animating width forces a page relayout every frame, so animate transform and opacity and stay on the compositor. A width from 12% to 100% and transform: scaleX() from 0.12 to 1 look identical in a design file, but in a side-by-side test one can run at 60fps and the other at 12 (illustrative figures; real devices vary). Good motion is invisible until it is wrong.

  • ✓transform-origin set to the trigger, so a menu grows out of the thing that opened it
  • ✓Animate transform and opacity only, never width, height or left
  • ✓prefers-reduced-motion swaps the movement for an opacity fade
  • ✓Interface motion inside the 150 to 250ms band, ease-out, with the bounce kept for celebrations
  • ×A 600ms animation
  • ×Animating width to draw a progress bar
  • ×A 300px fly-in for someone who asked for reduced motion
CSS
/* 4. origin: grow from the thing that opened it */
.menu { transform-origin: top left; } /* the trigger's corner, not the menu's own centre */
@keyframes menu-in { from { opacity: 0; transform: scale(.95); } to { opacity: 1; transform: none; } }
.menu.open { animation: menu-in 200ms ease-out both; } /* inside the 150 to 250ms band */

/* 5. reduced motion: a fade, never a flight */
@keyframes fly-in  { from { transform: translateX(300px); } to { transform: none; } }
@keyframes fade-in { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } }
.panel { animation: fly-in 200ms ease-out both; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .panel { animation-name: fade-in; } /* swap the 300px move for an opacity fade */
}

/* 6. the jank: animate transform and opacity, stay on the compositor */
.bar { width: 100%; transform-origin: left; }
.bar.loading { animation: fill 1.2s ease-out both; }
@keyframes fill { from { transform: scaleX(.12); } to { transform: scaleX(1); } } /* not width: 12% to 100%, which relayouts every frame */
A card becomes a page, one property
→
view-transition-name: hero on both
06

View Transitions

The View Transitions API morphs one state into another with no animation library. A card becomes a page: give the card image and the page header the same view-transition-name; the browser snapshots the old and new states and interpolates size, position and corner radius (in the demo width 379 to 1080px, top 201 to 64px, radius 15 to 0px). In a single-page app, one document.startViewTransition() call wraps the DOM update. Every row, its own name: give each list item a unique name and sorting or filtering slides every row with no animation code; one item, one name, because a duplicate name throws an InvalidStateError and the transition is skipped.

A theme toggle that spreads: animate ::view-transition-new(root) with a clip-path circle that grows from the click position, a circular wipe in one rule (600ms in the demo). A modal born from its button: the button holds the name, and on open the name moves to the dialog, so it grows out of the place that was tapped instead of fading in from nowhere. Across real page loads: @view-transition { navigation: auto; } on both pages gives the same morph on a multi-page site with no framework (Chrome 126+, Safari 18.2+); without support the page swaps instantly, so nothing breaks. Respect reduced motion by turning the animations off under prefers-reduced-motion.

  • ✓One shared name on the two states that should morph
  • ✓A unique name per list row
  • ✓Modals grow from the button that opened them
  • ✓Instant swap as the fallback, reduced motion honoured
  • ×An animation library for a morph the browser can do
  • ×Two elements sharing one name on the same page
CSS + JS
.card img, .page header { view-transition-name: hero; } /* same name, two snapshots */
document.startViewTransition(() => showPage()); // SPA: wrap the DOM update

li { view-transition-name: var(--trip); } /* <li style="--trip: trip-1">, one item, one name */

::view-transition-new(root) { animation: reveal 600ms; }
@keyframes reveal { from { clip-path: circle(0 at var(--x) var(--y)); } } /* --x, --y = click position */

btn.style.viewTransitionName = "share";
document.startViewTransition(() => {
  btn.style.viewTransitionName = "none";
  dialog.style.viewTransitionName = "share"; // the name moves to the dialog
  dialog.showModal();
});

@view-transition { navigation: auto; } /* on both pages: cross-document, no framework */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { ::view-transition-group(*) { animation: none; } }

Navigation

4 patterns

How someone moves through a product without losing their place.

Press Tab to move through, click leaves no ring
01

Focus States

Removing outline: none without putting a real replacement in its place is a genuine accessibility failure, not a legitimate style choice. It leaves keyboard users with no visible indication of where they are on the page at all. :focus-visible is the correct modern fix: it shows a focus ring only for keyboard navigation, keeping a mouse click free of the ring while Tab still gets one. Inside a modal, trap focus so Tab can’t escape to the page behind it, and explicitly return focus to the triggering element when the modal closes. Visual tab order needs to match DOM order; a CSS-only reorder that doesn’t match creates a genuinely confusing keyboard-navigation path.

  • ✓:focus-visible so clicks stay clean, Tab gets a ring
  • ×Visual order drifting from DOM order
CSS + JS
.btn:focus { outline: none; } /* mouse click: no ring */
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; } /* keyboard: real ring */

// focus trap: Tab/Shift+Tab cycle within the modal, never escape to the page behind it
modal.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;
  const focusable = [...modal.querySelectorAll('button, [href], input, [tabindex]')];
  const [first, last] = [focusable[0], focusable.at(-1)];
  if (e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) { e.preventDefault(); last.focus(); }
  else if (!e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) { e.preventDefault(); first.focus(); }
});
const triggerEl = document.activeElement;
closeModal(() => triggerEl.focus()); // focus returns to what opened it
Match the platform
02

Navigation Patterns

Bottom tabs are the mobile-native pattern for primary navigation (thumb-reachable, always visible); a persistent sidebar is the desktop-native pattern once a product has five or more top-level sections. Match the pattern to the platform’s own convention rather than personal taste. A bottom tab bar ported straight to desktop, or a sidebar squeezed onto mobile, both fight how people already expect to navigate on that device. A command palette (Cmd+K) supplements visible navigation for power users; it should never replace it, since not everyone knows the shortcut exists. Reserve breadcrumbs for genuinely nested hierarchies past two levels deep; a flat one- or two-level structure doesn’t need them.

  • ✓Command palette alongside visible nav, not instead
  • ×Burying primary nav in a desktop hamburger
CSS
.nav-mobile { display: none; }
.nav-desktop { display: flex; flex-direction: column; width: 240px; } /* persistent sidebar, 5+ sections */

@media (max-width: 768px) {
  .nav-desktop { display: none; } /* hamburger is NOT the mobile answer either, use tabs */
  .nav-mobile {
    display: flex; position: fixed; bottom: 0; inset-inline: 0;
    justify-content: space-around; padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom);
  } /* bottom tabs, thumb-reachable, always visible */
}
/* Cmd+K palette is ADDITIVE, .nav-desktop / .nav-mobile still render regardless of it existing */
Cursor-based, not offset
03

Pagination

Cursor-based pagination (a pointer to “the row after this ID”) stays stable even while rows are actively being inserted or deleted underneath it; offset-based pagination (“skip N rows”) silently duplicates or skips rows the instant the underlying dataset shifts between page loads, because “row 20” refers to a different row than it did a second ago. Keep the current page (or cursor) in the URL so a reload or a shared link lands on the same page instead of resetting to page one, and restore the scroll position when returning from a detail view back to a list.

  • ✓Page number lives in the URL
  • ×Rendering every page-number link, not truncated
JS
// cursor pagination, stable even while rows are being inserted/deleted concurrently
async function fetchPage(cursor) {
  const res = await api.get(`/items?after=${cursor ?? ''}&limit=20`);
  const url = new URL(location);
  url.searchParams.set('cursor', res.nextCursor); // lives in the URL, reload/share lands on the same page
  history.replaceState(null, '', url);
  return res.items;
}

// on returning from a detail view
sessionStorage.setItem('list-scroll', String(window.scrollY)); // saved before navigating away
window.scrollTo(0, Number(sessionStorage.getItem('list-scroll') ?? 0)); // restored on return
Indicator slides, never teleports
Tab content swaps with a fade, indicator glides to the new position
04

Tabs System

The active-tab indicator needs to physically slide from the old position to the new one, never teleport instantly. The slide is what tells the eye which direction the change moved in. When a tab row overflows the available width, it scrolls horizontally with an edge fade hinting more is there; it should never wrap onto a second line, which breaks the single-row mental model tabs depend on. Support full keyboard operation (arrow keys move between tabs, Home/End jump to the first/last), and fade the content out then back in on switch rather than a hard instant cut, which reads as a glitch. A desktop tab bar simply shrunk down rarely survives the transition to mobile without redesigning as its own pattern.

  • ✓Full keyboard operation (arrows/Home/End)
  • ×A shrunk desktop tab bar reused on mobile
CSS + JS
.tab-list { display: flex; overflow-x: auto; scrollbar-width: none; } /* scrolls, never wraps */
.tab-indicator {
  position: absolute; height: 2px; background: var(--accent);
  transition: transform 200ms var(--ease-out), width 200ms var(--ease-out); /* slides, never teleports */
}

tabList.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  const tabs = [...tabList.querySelectorAll('[role=tab]')];
  const i = tabs.indexOf(document.activeElement);
  if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') tabs[(i + 1) % tabs.length].focus();
  if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft') tabs[(i - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length].focus();
  if (e.key === 'Home') tabs[0].focus();
  if (e.key === 'End') tabs.at(-1).focus();
});

Content

4 patterns

The words and page-level structure that carry as much weight as any component.

Different copy per type
No projects yet
Create your first project
No results match your filters
Clear filters
Couldn't load projects
Retry
01

Empty States

A completely blank screen reads as broken to whoever lands on it. A small illustration or icon plus a short line of copy signals “this is intentionally empty,” not “something failed to load.” Give the screen exactly one clear primary CTA that names the actual next step (“Create your first project”), not a vague, generic action. Any empty state worth shipping answers three questions at once: why is this empty, what should the person do about it, and does the copy teach them something about the product rather than just stating a fact. Different causes need different copy, not one shared message. First-time use gets an onboarding CTA (“Create your first project”). A filtered or searched view that came back empty gets a clear-filter affordance (“No invoices match ‘overdue’, clear filter”). Missing permissions gets an explanation plus a real path forward (“You don't have access, ask your admin to share this”), not a dead end. Something genuinely empty by design gets a plain, calm confirmation (“All caught up, no pending reviews”) rather than treating an intentional zero like a problem. A bare “Try refreshing” as the only available action is rarely the real fix and reads as a shrug.

  • ✓One clear primary CTA, the actual next step
  • ✓Copy answers why it's empty and what to do, distinct per cause (first-run, filtered, permissions, by design)
  • ×A generic “Try refreshing” as the only action
Illustration, two variants. Variant A: a small illustration or icon plus a short line of copy (this entry). Use when: the design system has illustrations or icons ready for empty states. Variant B: text only, with the copy doing all the teaching. Use when: there is no illustration set yet, since a borrowed or generic picture is worse than none. Both are kept on purpose.
JS
const EMPTY_STATES = {
  'first-run': { copy: 'No projects yet', cta: { label: 'Create your first project', action: createProject } },
  'filtered':  { copy: 'No results match your filters', cta: { label: 'Clear filters', action: clearFilters } },
  'error':     { copy: "Couldn't load projects", cta: { label: 'Retry', action: reload } },
}; // distinct copy per type, never one generic message for all three

function renderEmpty(type) {
  const { copy, cta } = EMPTY_STATES[type];
  return `<EmptyIllustration /><p>${copy}</p><button onclick="${cta.action}">${cta.label}</button>`;
}
The fixed order
Hero
Proof
Problem
Solution
CTA
02

Landing Page Skeleton

Hero → Proof → Problem → Solution → CTA is the fixed order high-converting landing pages follow, because it mirrors how someone actually decides to trust a page: first orient (what is this), then trust (who else uses it), then feel the pain point, then see the fix, then act. The hero itself needs to answer what/who/why within about three seconds of landing, before anyone has scrolled at all. Repeat the same CTA at both the top and bottom of the page rather than making someone scroll all the way back up once they’re convinced. Burying social proof at the very bottom wastes it; it works hardest placed early, right after the hero.

  • ✓Hero answers what/who/why in ~3 seconds
  • ×Burying social proof at the bottom
HTML structure
<section class="hero">      <!-- answers what/who/why in ~3s -->
<section class="proof">     <!-- logos/testimonials, early, not buried at the bottom -->
<section class="problem">   <!-- the pain point, named specifically -->
<section class="solution">  <!-- how the product actually fixes it -->
<section class="cta-final"> <!-- SAME cta as the hero, not a scroll back up -->
Reward, not mechanic
Submit→Create my free account
Operation failed→Card declined, try a different card
03

Microcopy

A button label should name the actual reward someone gets (“Create my free account”), not the raw mechanic behind it (“Submit”). The reward-framed version measurably converts better because it answers “what happens when I click this” in the label itself. An error message should turn into a concrete next step, not just a diagnosis of what went wrong. Labels stay persistently visible above their field rather than vanishing as placeholder text once typing starts. Cold system-speak like “operation failed” or “an error occurred” reads as the product blaming an abstraction instead of a plain-language explanation.

  • ✓Errors turn into a next step, not just a diagnosis
  • ×Cold system-speak like “operation failed”
JS
const COPY = {
  submitBtn: 'Create my free account',        // names the reward, not "Submit"
  cardDeclined: 'Card declined, try a different card or contact your bank.', // diagnosis + next step
  networkError: "Couldn't save, check your connection and try again.", // never "operation failed"
};
// label: persistent, never placeholder-only, see Form Field States above
First and last carry the recall
LOGO
ProductPricingAbout
Sign up
04

Serial Position

Recall across any sequence is U-shaped: people remember the first items strongly (primacy), the last items strongly (recency), and forget almost everything sandwiched in the middle. A navbar puts the logo first and the primary CTA last for exactly this reason; both sit in the high-recall positions by construction. On a landing page or pricing list, lead with the single strongest selling point and close with the single strongest piece of proof, and never let a genuinely critical CTA end up stranded in the low-recall middle of a long list of options.

  • ✓Logo leads a navbar, primary CTA closes it
  • ×Burying a critical CTA in the low-recall middle
HTML structure
<nav>
  <div class="logo">...</div>          <!-- first position, high recall -->
  <div class="nav-links">...</div>     <!-- middle, lowest recall, least critical items go here -->
  <button class="cta-primary">Sign up</button> <!-- last position, high recall -->
</nav>
<!-- pricing list: strongest USP first, strongest proof/guarantee last, nothing critical in the middle -->

The Psychology of the User Experience

4 patterns

How people perceive, choose and remember. Everything here is a research-backed heuristic, not a law: each describes a tendency that holds often enough to design around, and each has limits. Fitts, Hick and Jakob have their full entries in this category; the other psychology-driven entries stay in the category where they already were, and the index at the end of this category points to every one of them by entry number.

Same action, two targets
Save
Big Save: easy to reach
Save
Small Save: harder to hit
01

Fitts’s Heuristic

Important buttons should be easy to reach, so a big Save button beats a small one. This is Fitts’s heuristic, often written up as “Fitts’s law”; it is a research-backed heuristic, not a law. Its practical side is already in Click Target Sizing (Interaction, entry 25): the 44 by 44 pixel touch zone and the 8 pixel gap between adjacent buttons.

  • ✓The important button (the Save) is big and easy to reach
  • ✓Apply the size and gap numbers in Click Target Sizing
  • ×A small, hard-to-reach button for the action that matters most
CSS
/* the important action is big and easy to reach: a big Save beats a small one (sizes are demo values) */
.btn-save { min-width: 120px; min-height: 44px; }

/* the touch-zone and gap floors from Click Target Sizing still apply to every other button */
.btn-row { display: flex; gap: 8px; }
.btn-row button { min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px; }
Same decision, more options
3 choices: fast to decide
15 choices: slow to decide
02

Hick’s Heuristic

The more choices there are, the longer it takes to decide: three choices are quick to pick from, fifteen are slow. This is Hick’s heuristic, often written up as “Hick’s law”; it is a research-backed heuristic, not a law.

Read it precisely. Decision time grows with the number of options; it does not say that fewer options is always better, so it is a cost to weigh against what people need to see, not an instruction to strip choices out. The related rules already in this library are Field Control Thresholds (Forms, entry 15), which picks the control from the option count, and Form Field Grouping (Forms, entry 14), which caps visible fields at seven.

  • ✓Weigh the number of options before designing the choice: more options, more time to decide (3 choices are quick, 15 are slow)
  • ✓Pair it with the option-count thresholds in Field Control Thresholds
  • ×Reading it as “fewer options is always better”; it says decision time grows with the number of options, nothing more
HTML
<!-- 3 choices: quick to decide, all visible -->
<fieldset>
  <label><input type="radio" name="plan"> Starter</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="plan"> Growth</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="plan"> Scale</label>
</fieldset>

<!-- 15 choices: decision time grows with the number of options; the control to use is in Field Control Thresholds -->
<select name="region"> <!-- 15 options --> </select>
Three products, one familiar layout
Photo app
Video app
Your app
03

Jakob’s Heuristic

Users expect your product to work like the products they already know. Picture the bottom bars of a photo app, a video app and “your app” all sharing the same layout. This is Jakob’s heuristic, often written up as “Jakob’s law”; it is a research-backed heuristic, not a law.

The rule already in this library that applies it is in Navigation Patterns (Navigation, entry 02): match the pattern to the platform’s own convention rather than personal taste.

  • ✓Reuse the layout and behaviour users already know from the products they use
  • ✓Match the platform’s own navigation convention (Navigation Patterns)
  • ×A product that behaves unlike the ones its users already know, with no reason to
CSS
/* the familiar mobile layout: a bottom bar with a few evenly spaced tabs, as in the apps people already use */
.tab-bar { position: fixed; bottom: 0; left: 0; right: 0; display: flex; justify-content: space-around; }
Same 10 digits, 4 memory slots
4155550123
10 items, 6 lost
415 555 0123
3 chunks, all kept
04

Chunking

Working memory holds about four chunks (Cowan, 2001), not the seven that is often quoted. Ten loose digits (4155550123) overflow four slots and six are lost; the same number in three groups (415 555 0123) fits, with all three chunks kept. Group anything people must hold in their heads while they act on it: phone numbers, card numbers, reference numbers, codes, long IDs, and the steps of a flow.

It is a research-backed heuristic about memory, not a law of layout. The rules in this library that apply it are Input Masking (Forms, entry 06), which formats as people type, and OTP Input (Forms, entry 07).

  • ✓Show and accept long numbers in groups of 3 to 4
  • ✓Keep what people must remember to about four chunks
  • ×A 10-digit reference shown as one unbroken string
JS
// show and type in chunks: 415 555 0123, not 4155550123
const chunk = (d, sizes = [3, 3, 4]) => { let i = 0; return sizes.map(n => d.slice(i, i += n)).filter(Boolean).join(' '); };
chunk('4155550123'); // "415 555 0123": 3 chunks fit 4 slots

Where every psychology-driven entry lives

Nothing here was moved, copied or deleted: each entry stays in its own category. Proximity and Von Restorff already had full entries in Visual, so they are pointed to rather than duplicated. Entry numbers are as shown in each category.

  • Psychology, 02Hick’s Heuristic more choices, more time to decide

  • Visual, 17Von Restorff Effect the element that is different gets noticed first

AI Slop: What Not To Do

9 patterns

The defaults that make an interface, a page or a piece of writing read as machine-made, gathered in one place so they can be checked for on purpose. Each entry leads with the thing not to do, says why it reads as generated, and gives the one-line fix. AI Dashboard Tells (Visual, entry 21), AI Landing Page Tells (Visual, entry 22) and Chat UI System (Interaction, entry 23) keep their full write-ups where they are; the entries here point to them and add no new tell. Read every entry as a stylistic baseline to deviate from deliberately, not as a test for who or what made something: the strongest pushback on these tells (major-brand tools also use shadows, per-card icon colours and gradients) is recorded under AI Dashboard Tells and applies to the whole category.

Standing rule for this category. Any new AI-slop tell goes here, not only in the Visual category.

01

Dashboard Tells

Don’t. Ship the five defaults nobody chose: a gradient header that encodes nothing, four accent colours on four stat tiles, every stat at the same size and weight, a shadow on every card, and a templated greeting next to a bare number.

Why it reads as machine-made. Each one is decoration or a default standing in for a decision. They are the five small habits that make a generated dashboard read as generated.

Fix. One line per tell in the list below. The full write-up, the demo and the CSS live in AI Dashboard Tells (Visual, entry 21), which stays where it is; this entry only points to it.

  • ×A decorative gradient header. Fix: one flat accent colour.
  • ×Four stat tiles in four colours. Fix: one shared tile colour, so the number is the hero.
  • ×Every stat at the same size and weight. Fix: one primary number and three visibly smaller secondaries.
  • ×A drop shadow on every card. Fix: shadow only on what floats (dropdown, popover, toast), a hairline border on the rest.
  • ×“Welcome back, Jordan” beside a bare “+12.5% from last month”. Fix: name the period, use tabular digits, and give the number a shape with a sparkline.
TEXT
review pass, dashboard (details and CSS: Visual, entry 21)
[ ] gradient header that encodes nothing         -> one flat accent
[ ] four accent colours on four stat tiles       -> one shared tile colour
[ ] every stat the same size and weight          -> one primary, three secondary
[ ] a shadow on every card                       -> shadow only on what floats
[ ] "Welcome back, Jordan" and a bare delta      -> name the period, tabular digits, a sparkline
Same hero, five defaults removed

02

Landing Page Tells

Don’t. Ship the landing-page version of the same habit: an adjective stacked on a vague noun as the headline, a big ambient glow behind the hero, two equal-weight buttons, a trust number nobody can check, and a row of icon-plus-adjective feature cards.

Why it reads as machine-made. It is the dashboard habit on a different surface, decoration standing in for a real decision, so nothing on the page is attached to the actual product.

Fix. One line per tell below. The full write-up, the demo and the CSS live in AI Landing Page Tells (Visual, entry 22), which stays where it is.

  • ×A headline that stacks an adjective on a vague noun (“Supercharge your workflow with AI”). Fix: state the outcome in plain text.
  • ×A big ambient gradient glow behind the hero. Fix: put the colour on the product screenshot itself.
  • ×Two equal-weight calls to action, especially both left-aligned in a row. Fix: one true primary, one visibly quieter secondary.
  • ×“Trusted by 10,000+ teams” with no attribution. Fix: one named quote with a role and a face.
  • ×Feature cards that are an icon plus an adjective (a lightning bolt beside “Fast”). Fix: a card that shows the real product screen doing the thing.
TEXT
review pass, landing page (details and CSS: Visual, entry 22)
[ ] adjective + vague noun headline              -> the outcome, in plain text
[ ] ambient glow behind the hero                 -> colour on the product screenshot
[ ] two equal-weight calls to action             -> one primary, one quieter secondary
[ ] "Trusted by 10,000+ teams", no attribution   -> one named quote, role and face
[ ] icon + adjective feature cards               -> the real product screen in the card

03

Typography Tells

Don’t. Set one line height on everything, so a large heading and a paragraph of body text share the same leading.

Why it reads as machine-made. The same line height everywhere is often called an “AI tell”. That claim is plausible but unverified.

Fix. Let line height move opposite to size: about 1.1 on headings and about 1.5 on body text. The fix is ordinary typographic practice whether or not the tell claim holds; it is rule 5 of Typography as a System (Visual, entry 24).

  • ✓About 1.1 on headings and about 1.5 on body text, because the rule stands on its own.
  • ×The same line height on headings and body text (often called an AI tell; unverified).
One tell here, and it is unverified. Of the seven rules in Typography as a System, only the line-height one is called an AI tell. The other six (one font family, five sizes on one ratio, three text colours, two weights, letter spacing, and a 45 to 75 character measure with tabular figures) are its defaults for a considered type system, not tells, so they are not repeated as tells here.
CSS
/* don't: one line height on everything (often called an AI tell; unverified) */
body, h1, h2, p { line-height: 1.4; }

/* fix: line height moves opposite to size */
h1, h2 { line-height: 1.1; }
p      { line-height: 1.5; }

04

Chat UI Tells

Don’t. Leave a chat thread on its defaults: messages from one sender not grouped, a timestamp on every bubble, a spinner while a sent message waits for the server, a list that jumps to the bottom whenever something arrives, a typing indicator pinned away from the thread, and a composer that keeps growing until it pushes the thread out of view.

Why it reads as machine-made. Each is a default nobody decided; Chat UI System says a thread reads as considered or as generated on these six decisions. Treat this family as unconsidered rather than proven generated.

Fix. One line per decision below. The full write-up and the code live in Chat UI System (Interaction, entry 23), which stays where it is.

  • ×No grouping, so the eye re-parses who is talking on every line. Fix: one avatar per run, about 4px inside a group and about 16px between senders.
  • ×A timestamp printed on every bubble. Fix: a relative date divider, with the exact time on hover.
  • ×A spinner while the sent message waits on the server. Fix: the bubble lands first (optimistic send).
  • ×A list that jumps to the bottom when a message arrives. Fix: a “new messages” pill, and auto-scroll only if the person was already at the bottom.
  • ×A typing indicator in a fixed status line away from the thread. Fix: show it inline, in the sender’s own row.
  • ×A composer that grows forever. Fix: grow to about five lines, then scroll inside the box.
TEXT
review pass, chat UI (details and CSS: Interaction, entry 23)
[ ] messages from one sender not grouped         -> one avatar per run, 4px inside, 16px between
[ ] a timestamp on every bubble                  -> date divider, exact time on hover
[ ] a spinner while a sent message waits         -> the bubble lands first
[ ] the list jumps to the bottom on arrival      -> "new messages" pill
[ ] a typing indicator away from the thread      -> inline, in the sender's own row
[ ] a composer that grows forever                -> about five lines, then it scrolls
Choreography against a plain verdict
Flourish: about a second after the last digit
Neutral while typing, green only on a correct code
05

Decorative Motion Tells

Don’t. Add choreography that plays after the job is already done and makes the person wait for it. In one popular OTP demo, four digit boxes swing onto a ring, spin a turn and a quarter and settle into one green tile after the code has been typed, about a second of delay. The same family is decoration that carries no information, such as a glowing network-graph animation that looks impressive and says nothing.

Why it reads as machine-made. This is a judgement about reception, not a rule. The OTP flourish is widely received as too much and machine-made, and a glowing network graph invites the question of whether it means anything at all.

Fix. Motion has to carry information and never delay the task. Keep the interface neutral until a verdict, show colour only when the code is right or wrong, and keep interface motion in the 150 to 250ms band with the bounce saved for a celebration. The motion rules that hold this line are in Animation Timing (Motion, entry 01), Easing Curves (Motion, entry 03) and Motion That Stays Cheap (Motion, entry 05).

  • ✓Neutral UI until a verdict: green only when the code is correct, red only when it is wrong.
  • ✓Interface motion in the 150 to 250ms band, ease-out, with the bounce kept for a celebration.
  • ×A choreographed flourish after the task is done, adding about a second of delay.
  • ×A glowing, animated visual that carries no information.
Audience reaction, not proof. Audience reaction shows how a piece of motion is received, not how it was made. The OTP animation itself is a sound, established CSS technique (see OTP Input, Forms, entry 07); the objection is to the delay and the flourish, not the technique.
CSS
/* don't: about a second of choreography after the code is already typed */

/* fix: colour is reserved for verdicts, neutral while the code is being entered */
.otp-box            { border-color: var(--border); }
.otp-box.is-correct { border-color: var(--ok); }
.otp-box.is-wrong   { border-color: var(--bad); }

/* fix: interface motion in the 150 to 250ms band, ease-out; the bounce is for a celebration */
.menu.open { animation: menu-in 200ms ease-out both; }
Words a model is said to be told never to use
genuinelyhonestlystraightforward
Not a tool, not a platform, not a budget line.
The negation pivot: state what is true, then stop.
06

Writing and Copy Tells

Don’t. Write with the fingerprints of machine text: the three words a model is said to be told never to use (genuinely, honestly, straightforward), the “not X, not Y, but Z” pivot, and the social-post hooks and beats. In an interface the same defaults show up as templated copy: a personalised greeting beside a bare number, an adjective-plus-noun headline, and a trust number nobody can check. Those three are covered in Visual, entries 21 and 22.

Why it reads as machine-made. The word list carries the stated reason that a word which insists on honesty reads as the opposite, so the instruction is to state the point and stop. The negation pivot is a dead giveaway; it comes in three shapes, the drumbeat triad (“Not a tool, not a platform, not a budget line. A person.”), the reversal (“It is not mysterious. It is ten jobs.”) and the appositive pivot (“a figure, not an adjective”). Social-post hooks and beats make a draft read as ghost-written or generated.

Fix. State the thing that is true and stop. Lead with a fact or a specific detail only the author would know, close with a request or a link rather than a tidy two-beat, and apply one test: if the draft would be equally plausible under 50 other people’s names, it is too generic.

  • ✓State the point and stop; lead with a specific fact; keep plain factual negation.
  • ×The words genuinely, honestly and straightforward (said to be banned outright in an extracted AI system prompt; unverified).
  • ×The negation pivot: the drumbeat triad, the reversal and the appositive pivot.
  • ×Hero-line openers and hooks (“X is broken.”, “Here’s the thing.”, “Here’s why this matters.”, a rhetorical question).
  • ×Rule-of-three beats, parallel negation lists (“No layers, no gatekeepers, no waiting.”), “The bar is simple.” setups, a tidy two-part closer, and every sentence on its own line for effect.
Partly unverified. The three words come from a publicly shared copy of an extracted AI system prompt; that copy’s authenticity and completeness are unconfirmed, and the claim that banning them makes output stop sounding machine-made is untested. The pivot and the hooks and beats are editing judgements from draft reviews, not researched claims. Plain factual negation (“the technology does not supervise itself”) is not the tell; the reflexive antithesis used as a constant cadence is.
TEXT
sweep list, writing and copy
words (from an extracted AI prompt, unverified)
  genuinely   honestly   straightforward

negation pivot, three shapes (plain factual negation stays)
  drumbeat triad     "Not a tool, not a platform, not a budget line. A person."
  reversal           "It is not mysterious. It is ten jobs."
  appositive pivot   "a figure, not an adjective"

hooks and beats
  "X is broken."   "Here's the thing."   "Here's why this matters."   a rhetorical-question opener
  rule of three   parallel negation list   "The bar is simple."   a tidy two-part closer   one sentence per line

test: would this draft be equally plausible under 50 other people's names? If yes, it is too generic.

07

Pricing Page Tells

Don’t. Ship three identical tier cards, a Popular badge on every one, twelve repeated check marks per card, a gradient button on each plan, and a percent-off chip as the only statement of the saving.

Why it reads as machine-made. Each one is the default of a generator that was never asked to recommend anything: three equal cards are no recommendation, and a badge on every card is a badge on none.

Fix. One line per tell in the list below. The full write-up, with the numbers and the percent versus dollars variants, lives in Pricing Table (Visual, entry 27); this entry only points to it.

  • ×Three identical tiers. Fix: one tier highlighted, two quiet.
  • ×A badge on every card. Fix: one badge, no runner-up badges.
  • ×Twelve repeated checks per tier. Fix: list the difference (Everything in Starter, plus).
  • ×A gradient button on every plan. Fix: one filled button, the rest outlined, labels naming the plan or action.
  • ×A bare -17% chip. Fix: show the saving in the unit that reads bigger (percent under about $100, dollars over), with the old price struck through.
TEXT
review pass, pricing page (details and CSS: Visual, entry 27)
[ ] three identical tier cards                 -> one highlighted, two quiet
[ ] a badge on every card                      -> one badge, no runner-up
[ ] twelve repeated checks per tier            -> list the difference
[ ] a gradient button on every plan            -> one filled, the rest outlined
[ ] a bare percent chip                        -> the unit that reads bigger, old price struck
Same empty state, the tells removed

08

Copy That Reads Machine-Made

Don’t. Ship interface copy with four habits of machine text. Heading echo: the first sentence restates the heading, so the reader spends a line learning nothing. Fake candour: openers such as Honestly?, Here’s the thing and Let’s be real, which perform frankness instead of delivering a fact. Strawman openers: This isn’t about X. It’s about Y., which knocks down a claim nobody made before getting to the point. Fake options: a set of choices nobody would pick, laid out so one looks obvious, which reads as manipulation the moment anyone notices.

Why it reads as machine-made. Each one is filler shaped like emphasis. It adds a beat of rhythm and no information, and once a reader spots one they start discounting the rest of the screen. The strawman is a close cousin of the negation pivot in Writing and Copy Tells (entry 06), and fake candour overlaps its hero-line hooks; this entry covers how the same habits show up in interface copy: headings, empty states, settings and plan pickers.

Fix. Make the first sentence carry new information. Cut the candour opener and keep the fact that followed it. Open with the claim itself, not the claim you are not making. Offer only options someone could genuinely want, and when one is recommended, say so plainly with a Recommended label and the reason.

  • ✓Under the heading Invoices: “Nothing sent yet. Your first invoice takes about a minute.”
  • ✓“Export to CSV or PDF. Large reports arrive by email.”
  • ✓“Backups run every night and are kept for 30 days.”
  • ✓“Turn on backups” beside “Not now”, with a Recommended label and the reason on the first.
  • ×Heading echo. Under the heading Invoices: “Invoices help you manage your invoices.”
  • ×Fake candour. “Honestly? Exporting is easy.”
  • ×Strawman opener. “This isn’t about storage. It’s about peace of mind.”
  • ×Fake options. “Keep my data safe” beside “No thanks, I like losing my work.”
TEXT
review pass, interface copy
[ ] the first sentence restates the heading        -> make it carry new information
[ ] Honestly? / Here's the thing / Let's be real   -> cut the opener, keep the fact
[ ] This isn't about X. It's about Y.              -> open with Y
[ ] options nobody would pick                      -> real options, a plain Recommended label

Quick Checklist

Don’t. Ship a screen, a page or a piece of copy that trips any of these lines without having decided it on purpose. This is the whole category as one line per tell, grouped by family, for a fast review pass. The fix for each line is in the entry for its family above. Two lines are marked unverified, where the original claim has not been checked.

  • ✓Add every new tell here as one line the moment it is spotted, in the entry for its family.
  • ×Dashboard. A gradient header that encodes nothing.
  • ×Dashboard. Four accent colours on four stat tiles.
  • ×Dashboard. Every stat at the same size and weight.
  • ×Dashboard. A drop shadow on every card.
  • ×Dashboard. A templated greeting and a bare delta (“Welcome back, Jordan”, “+12.5% from last month”).
  • ×Landing page. An adjective-plus-noun headline (“Supercharge your workflow with AI”).
  • ×Landing page. An ambient glow behind the hero.
  • ×Landing page. Two equal-weight calls to action, both left-aligned.
  • ×Landing page. A trust number nobody can check (“Trusted by 10,000+ teams”).
  • ×Landing page. Icon-plus-adjective feature cards.
  • ×Typography. One line height on everything (unverified).
  • ×Chat UI. Messages from one sender not grouped.
  • ×Chat UI. A timestamp on every bubble.
  • ×Chat UI. A spinner while a sent message waits for the server.
  • ×Chat UI. A list that jumps to the bottom on every new message.
  • ×Chat UI. A typing indicator away from the thread.
  • ×Chat UI. A composer that grows until it pushes the thread out of view.
  • ×Decorative motion. Choreography after the job is done (the OTP orbit flourish).
  • ×Decorative motion. A glowing visual that carries no information.
  • ×Writing. The words genuinely, honestly and straightforward (unverified source).
  • ×Writing. The negation pivot (“not X, not Y, but Z”).
  • ×Writing. Hero-line openers and hooks (“X is broken.”, “Here’s the thing.”).
  • ×Writing. Rule-of-three beats, parallel negation lists and one sentence per line.
  • ×Writing. A first sentence that restates the heading (heading echo).
  • ×Writing. Fake candour openers (“Honestly?”, “Here’s the thing”, “Let’s be real”).
  • ×Writing. Strawman openers (“This isn’t about X. It’s about Y.”).
  • ×Writing. Fake options nobody would pick, laid out so one looks obvious.
  • ×Pricing. Three identical pricing tiers.
  • ×Pricing. A badge on every pricing card.
  • ×Pricing. Twelve repeated check marks per tier.
  • ×Pricing. A gradient button on every plan.
  • ×Pricing. A bare percent chip as the only statement of the saving.
  • ×Cards. A card around everything; a form section is not a card (fix in Card Treatment System, Visual entry 28).
A review aid, not a detector. A hit means a default nobody decided, not proof that a machine made it.
